title: Amazon S3 Express One Zone
content:
← Back to Articles AWS / Cloud Computing AMAZON S3 EXPRESS ONE ZONE – UP TO 10X FASTER, BUT IS THE SYSTEM TRULY MORE EFFICIENT? View post on AWS Study Group VN community 18/10/2026 Figure 1: Architectural model of Amazon S3 Express One Zone utilizing Directory Buckets co-located within the identical Availability Zone as EC2 / GPU compute clusters. In modern AI/ML and Data Analytics architectures, ingesting and processing millions of images or unstructured files requires continuous high-frequency access to Amazon S3. When data read speeds cannot keep pace with CPU/GPU processing capabilities, the system encounters an I/O Bottleneck — expensive compute clusters sit idle waiting for bytes, inflating execution time and infrastructure costs. To eliminate this friction, AWS introduced Amazon S3 Express One Zone, a specialized high-performance storage class engineered for ultra-low latency workloads.
1. What is Amazon S3 Express One Zone? Amazon S3 Express One Zone is the highest-performing storage class within Amazon S3, purpose-built to accelerate data-intensive analytics and machine learning model training workloads. Instead of standard general-purpose buckets, S3 Express One Zone operates on a newly re-architected Directory Bucket model.
The pivotal architectural distinction lies in data locality: Rather than replicating and dispersing objects across a minimum of three Availability Zones (Multi-AZ) like S3 Standard, S3 Express One Zone co-locates data within a single, dedicated Availability Zone (Single-AZ) of your choice. This enables architects to place high-throughput compute instances (such as Amazon EC2, Amazon EKS, or SageMaker GPU workers) inside the identical AZ as your storage, completely eliminating cross-AZ network transit latency and inter-AZ data transfer fees.
According to official AWS benchmarks, S3 Express One Zone consistently achieves single-digit millisecond access latencies (typically ranging between 1ms and 3ms) and throughput up to 10x faster than S3 Standard under sustained, concurrent request workloads.
Core Technical Concepts: Directory Bucket: A re-engineered hierarchical bucket architecture designed for ultra-low latency metadata lookups and high request rates.Single Availability Zone (Single-AZ): Localized storage placement delivering sub-10ms latency comparable to high-performance local network storage.Fast Session-Based Authentication: Lightweight, session-based security credentials that remove signature verification overhead on high-frequency API calls. 2. Advantages & Limitations Every cloud architectural decision represents a deliberate trade-off. To effectively leverage S3 Express One Zone, engineers must evaluate both its raw performance gains and its operational boundaries:
Architectural Criteria Amazon S3 Standard Amazon S3 Express One Zone Data Locality Multi-AZ (Minimum 3 AZs across region) Single-AZ (Co-located with compute) Access Latency Tens of milliseconds Single-digit milliseconds (1ms – 3ms) Relative Throughput Baseline reference (1x) Up to 10x faster Bucket Model General Purpose Bucket Directory Bucket Authentication Model Per-request signature (IAM / SigV4) Fast Session-Based Authentication Pricing Structure Lower baseline capacity cost per GB/mo Higher GB/mo and API request fees Advanced Feature Support Full support: Versioning, CRR, Lifecycle Versioning, CRR, Lifecycle not supported Core Advantages Sub-10ms Access Latency: Delivers single-digit millisecond read/write latencies, dramatically reducing turnaround time for high-frequency I/O workloads.Eliminates I/O Wait on Expensive Compute: Drastically reduces CPU/GPU idle wait cycles, ensuring costly machine learning accelerators operate at maximum utilization.Potential to Lower Compute Bills: Accelerating batch processing times allows organizations to shut down pricey EC2/GPU compute clusters earlier, generating net cost savings.Seamless AWS API Compatibility: Retains standard S3 API compatibility, enabling frictionless integration with PyTorch, TensorFlow, Apache Spark, and AWS SDKs without code refactoring. Limitations & Caveats Single-AZ Durability Model: Data is restricted to a single Availability Zone. In the rare event of a datacenter-level outage within that specific AZ, data is not redundantly available elsewhere like S3 Standard.Higher Unit Cost Structure: Storage capacity fees per GB/month and API request charges (PUT/GET) are significantly higher than S3 Standard. Viability hinges on workload access density.Lack of Certain S3 Enterprise Features: Does not currently support S3 Versioning, S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR/SRR), or automated S3 Lifecycle tiering.Amdahl's Law Reality: A 10x acceleration in storage I/O does not equate to a 10x acceleration of the end-to-end processing pipeline. 3. Performance Analysis via Example (Amdahl's Law) To definitively answer whether the system is truly more efficient, let us examine a quantitative scenario modeling an AI image processing pipeline based on Amdahl's Law:
1. Baseline System (Using Amazon S3 Standard): Fetching raw images from S3: 20 minutes (20% of total runtime) Preprocessing, feature extraction, GPU inference: 80 minutes (80% of total runtime) Total Baseline Time: 20 + 80 = 100 minutes 2. Upgraded to Amazon S3 Express One Zone (10x Faster I/O): New Storage Read Time: 20 minutes ÷ 10 = 2 minutes Compute Processing Time: 80 minutes (remains unchanged as CPU/GPU processing capability is unchanged) New Total Runtime: 2 minutes + 80 minutes = 82 minutes Execution Stage S3 Standard (Baseline) S3 Express One Zone Improvement Data Read Time (I/O) 20 minutes (20%) 2 minutes (2.4%) 10x Faster (-90%) Compute & Processing 80 minutes (80%) 80 minutes (97.6%) 0% (Unchanged) Total End-to-End Time 100 minutes 82 minutes 18% faster (Speedup 1.22x) Even though storage I/O was accelerated by a massive 10x (shrinking from 20 minutes down to 2 minutes), the total end-to-end runtime only dropped from 100 minutes to 82 minutes — representing an overall system gain of just 18%!
Amdahl's Law Speedup Formula:
Speedup(overall) = 1 / [ (1 - Fraction_enhanced) + (Fraction_enhanced / Speedup_component) ]
Speedup = 1 / [ (1 - 0.20) + (0.20 / 10) ]
Speedup = 1 / [ 0.80 + 0.02 ]
Speedup = 1 / 0.82 ≈ 1.22x (Equivalent to ~18% end-to-end runtime reduction) Crucial Technical Insight: Amdahl's Law states: The overall performance speedup of a system is strictly bounded by the proportion of time spent in the component being improved. Cloud architects must perform rigorous profiling before committing to premium storage tiers to determine whether the bottleneck is genuinely I/O-bound or compute-bound.
4. Architectural Perspectives & Recommendations (Two-Tier Storage) Based on these empirical insights, rather than prematurely migrating an entire Data Lake to S3 Express One Zone (incurring unnecessary storage expenses and losing Multi-AZ disaster durability), the recommended pattern is a Two-Tier Storage Architecture:
Layer 1: Amazon S3 Standard Master Data Lake Houses the persistent, authoritative master dataset with 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability across multiple Availability Zones. Provides disaster resilience and lowest cost per GB. → Layer 2: S3 Express One Zone Active Working Set / Scratchpad Temporarily stages only the active working set needed for the current batch training epoch. Co-located in the same AZ Directory Bucket for sub-10ms access speeds. ↔ Compute Layer: EC2 / GPU Nodes Co-located Compute Clusters Training workers are spun up inside the identical AZ as the S3 Express One Zone Directory Bucket, achieving maximum network throughput and zero cross-AZ data fees. Real-world Case Study: An AI vision pipeline maintains 1,000,000 reference images, but daily training iterations only require an active working set of 100,000 images. Instead of migrating all 1 million files, the orchestration layer syncs only the 100,000 active images to S3 Express One Zone before the run, wiping the scratchpad after completion.
Investment Break-Even Formula (ROI Equation):
Data Staging Cost + Transfer Overhead < Compute (GPU/EC2) Cost Savings If data staging costs and time overhead exceed the financial savings gained from reduced GPU instance hours, keeping the files in S3 Standard with tuned multi-part reads or local RAM caching may remain the superior, cost-effective architecture.
5. Conclusion & Architectural Principles Amazon S3 Express One Zone represents a transformative leap for machine learning, real-time analytics, and latency-critical cloud workflows requiring sustained, high-frequency object access.
However, true architectural excellence is never defined by headline speeds like '10x faster'. Seasoned cloud architects must isolate which working set genuinely requires acceleration, project end-to-end system speedup through Amdahl's Law, and calculate the cost break-even threshold between storage and compute.
“Cloud architectural excellence does not lie in adopting the fastest individual service, but in selecting the right tool for each distinct phase of the workload.” 4-Step Pre-Flight Migration Checklist: 1. System Profiling: Profile I/O Wait vs. Compute time. Migrate only when I/O represents the primary execution bottleneck.2. Isolate Working Set: Stage hot working data into S3 Express One Zone while maintaining master datasets on S3 Standard.3. AZ Co-location: Ensure compute instances (EC2 / EKS / SageMaker) reside in the exact same AZ as the Directory Bucket.4. Financial ROI Check: Verify that incremental storage and API costs remain strictly lower than the compute savings achieved. Event Information AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 was a major one-day flagship conference organized by Amazon Web Services (AWS), bringing together solutions architects, lead engineers, enterprise technology executives, and government representatives in Vietnam.
Official Event Name: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 Date: Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Main Venue: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi, Hanoi, Vietnam Actual Participation: Watched the live stream from Hanoi at the FCAJ HCMC Watch Party in Ho Chi Minh City, actively participating in technical discussions with peers and mentors. Main Event Schedule (UTC+7) Time Activity 07:30 Check-in, badge collection, and Expo opening 09:00 Opening Keynote (KEY001) at Grand Ballroom, JW Marriott Hanoi 10:15 Networking break and technology exhibition exploration 11:00 Morning technical breakout sessions 12:05 Networking lunch and partner showcase 13:10 Early afternoon specialized technical tracks 14:50 Technical break and consultations with AWS specialists 15:20 Late afternoon deep-dive sessions 17:00 Event close At the FCAJ HCMC Watch Party, attendees joined the live stream of the KEY001 keynote at 09:00 and engaged directly with the DVT205 (HCMC Watch Party) session, which matched the topic of DVT203 (Building software like never before with agentic AI) held in Grand Ballroom 3 in Hanoi.
04 4. Main Topics & Technical Activities 4.1. Keynote and Agentic AI in Software Development Keynote KEY001: Framed around solving ambitious technological challenges with cloud and AI primitives, highlighting three core directions: embedding AI agents in software pipelines, workload modernization, and defense-in-depth system security. DVT205 / DVT203 (Building software like never before with agentic AI): Detailed how autonomous AI agents actively assist developers throughout the software lifecycle, from requirements analysis and code generation to automated testing and code review. Transitioning from Demo to Production: Sessions AIM201 (From Demo to Deployment) and AIM301 (Scaling Multi-Agent Architectures) addressed practical hurdles in operationalizing AI agents; PRT301-S and PRT201-S emphasized human governance, reliability, and security guardrails. 4.2. Data Analytics and AI-Ready Infrastructure Building AI-Ready Data Foundations: Sessions ANT202 and ANT211 established the critical necessity of authoritative data quality, cataloging, and low-latency access before deploying generative AI models. Financial Services Industry Applications: ANT201 provided builder guidance on data-driven agents for FSI, complemented by ANT214 highlighting VPBank's experience scaling enterprise data on Amazon Redshift. Unifying Siloed Data: ANT205 demonstrated cross-silo analytics using Amazon Quick Suite to derive complete business insights. 4.3. Application Modernization and Cloud Security Internal Developer Platforms on EKS: DEV205 illustrated platform engineering at scale on Amazon EKS; DEV208 shared lessons from migrating NestJS workloads from EC2/PM2 to EKS powered by GitOps. Monolith to Microservices: MAM203 outlined structured patterns for decomposing monolithic services onto EKS; AIM303 introduced AWS Transform AI Agent to automate the modernization of .NET and SQL Server workloads. Workload Identity & AppSec: DEV401 explored advanced workload identity engineering; DVT305 showcased AWS Security Agent for proactive security from code to production; AIM203 addressed multi-tier defense in depth for agentic systems. 4.4. Cloud Operations and Cost Optimization Storage Cost Optimization: DEV204, contributed by FCAJ, provided practical strategies for mastering Amazon S3 Storage Classes to eliminate unnecessary cloud expenditure. Infrastructure Drift Remediation: DEV206 detailed multi-agent workflows for automated drift detection and correction in Terraform / IaC repositories. Amazon Bedrock Spend Governance: DEV210 analyzed real-time cost control mechanisms and spend enforcement for enterprise Amazon Bedrock deployments at scale. Observability in the GenAI Era: PRT203-S (Datadog) detailed monitoring strategies beyond traditional golden signals for non-deterministic AI workloads. 05 5. Knowledge & Lessons Learned Key takeaways and technical insights acquired from the conference tracks:
Core Domain Key Insights & Engineering Principles 1. AI Reliability & Security Define explicit boundaries, evaluation metrics, and verification mechanisms before deploying autonomous agents. Ensure strict guardrails against hallucinations, measure error rates, and mandate human-in-the-loop sign-off for state-modifying actions. 2. Data Quality Authoritative, well-governed, and continuously refreshed data is the non-negotiable foundation for intelligent agents and analytics workloads. 3. Cloud Architecture Align application modernization with concrete operational bottlenecks: leverage containerization (Amazon ECS/EKS) and declarative GitOps delivery to shorten release cycles and minimize deployment blast radius. 4. Monitoring & Cost Integrate operational observability and cost tracking into system architecture from day one. Apply lifecycle tiering to Amazon S3 data and continuously track token spend and inference latency on Amazon Bedrock. Application to Nutrition E-Commerce Project The architectural concepts gained from the conference directly inform our group capstone project, Nutrition E-Commerce:
Amazon Bedrock for Nutrition Extraction: Deploying foundation models on Amazon Bedrock to extract nutritional profiles and allergen data from food label uploads, accompanied by a verification UI where users confirm extracted information before database persistence. S3 Storage Lifecycle Optimization: Applying automated S3 Lifecycle policies to product imagery and inspection documents, transitioning files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and archiving historical compliance logs to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days. Microservices on Amazon ECS Fargate: Containerizing the core product catalog and nutritional recommendation APIs onto serverless AWS Fargate, paired with automated Application Load Balancer health checks for high service availability. Identity & Cost Control: Enforcing least-privilege IAM roles and Workload Identity for containerized services, encrypting sensitive personal dietary records with AWS KMS, and implementing CloudWatch budget alerts on Amazon Bedrock invocation costs. 06 6. Personal Reflection Attending the live broadcast of AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 from the FCAJ HCMC Watch Party in Ho Chi Minh City provided immense technical value and inspiration. Participating in discussions alongside fellow student builders and experienced AWS community mentors helped bridge theoretical cloud concepts with enterprise realities.
Presentations from enterprise leaders (Techcombank, VPBank, Katalon, and AWS) reinforced that sustainable AI adoption requires more than proof-of-concept demos—it demands dependable data engineering, robust container platforms, strict governance, and real-time operational discipline. These takeaways directly guided my contributions to our team project and elevated the technical rigor of this internship report.

title: Workshop Overview
content:
Technical Workshop Guide Deploying Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS Hands-on Deployment Guide: Spring Boot 4, React 19, ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL, Bedrock AI & Terraform
A comprehensive step-by-step practical lab guide enabling engineers and students to deploy an end-to-end cloud-native nutrition e-commerce platform on Amazon Web Services. The entire infrastructure is automated via Terraform, running containerized Spring Boot 4 backend on serverless ECS Fargate, managed PostgreSQL on RDS, and generative AI intent parsing with Amazon Bedrock Nova 2 Lite. 5.1 Overview 5.2 Prerequisites 5.3 Core Infra 5.4 App Deployment 5.5 Bedrock AI 5.6 Monitoring & Cost 5.7 Clean-up 5.1. Workshop Overview Building a Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS This workshop guides you through deploying a cloud-native nutrition e-commerce platform on AWS using React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL, integrated with Amazon Bedrock for natural language food search. Learners will practice provisioning infrastructure, deploying application workloads, integrating AI capabilities, monitoring systems, and managing AWS cloud costs. Workshop Objectives Understand cloud web application architecture on AWS. Deploy frontend, backend, and managed database tiers. Integrate Amazon Bedrock for AI-assisted nutritional queries. Establish monitoring, security controls, and cost optimization. Overall Architecture Overall Architecture Diagram of Nutrition E-Commerce on AWS. The React application is distributed globally via CloudFront and S3. API requests are routed through an Application Load Balancer to Spring Boot on ECS Fargate. PostgreSQL is hosted on Amazon RDS, Cognito manages user authentication, and Amazon Bedrock powers nutritional intent extraction. Core application infrastructure is hosted in Singapore, with Bedrock and Guardrails operating in Tokyo. Workshop Roadmap 5.2. Prerequisites: Prepare AWS Account and developer toolchain. 5.3. Core Infrastructure: Provision cloud resources using Terraform. 5.4. Application Deployment: Deploy React and Spring Boot to AWS. 5.5. Amazon Bedrock: Integrate AI conversational nutrition search. 5.6. Monitoring & Cost: Configure observability, security, and budgets. 5.7. Resource Cleanup: Stop or tear down resources after the workshop. Expected Outcome Upon completing this workshop, learners will be capable of deploying, operating, and testing an AI-enabled nutrition e-commerce system on AWS while understanding how to monitor and control cloud expenditures. 5.2 Prerequisites → 5.2 – Prerequisites & Environment Setup Before deploying the Nutrition E-Commerce platform on AWS, learners must prepare an AWS account, developer toolchains, IAM access permissions, and a remote storage backend for Terraform State. This hands-on lab guides you through environment verification, configuring AWS IAM Identity Center, and bootstrapping the Terraform Backend on Amazon S3. 5.2.1. Tooling Preparation The table below lists the required developer toolchains and runtimes: Tool Requirement AWS Account Permissions to configure required AWS services (VPC, ECS, RDS, IAM, CloudFront, Bedrock) AWS CLI Version 2 (AWS CLI v2.x) Terraform Version ≥ 1.10 (tested with Terraform v1.10.5) Java JDK 21 (Eclipse Temurin or OpenJDK 21) Node.js & npm Compatible with repository (Node.js ≥ 20.x or 22.x LTS, npm ≥ 10.x) Docker Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with multi-platform container build support (linux/arm64) Git Source code version control (Git ≥ 2.40.x) PowerShell PowerShell 7 or Windows PowerShell for running verification commands and lifecycle scripts on Windows 5.2.2. Configure AWS Access & IAM Infrastructure provisioning adheres strictly to the Least Privilege principle with the following IAM components: AWS IAM Identity Center: Centrally manages user authentication and role assignments to AWS accounts via Single Sign-On (SSO). Permission set nutrition-plan: Attached with AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess, used for daily inspection, syntax validation, and planning (terraform plan). Permission set nutrition-apply: Combines ReadOnlyAccess with an inline policy from nutrition-apply-policy.json to apply approved infrastructure changes. Policy nutrition-boundary: Enforces a maximum permission boundary (nutrition-boundary-policy.json) on all IAM roles generated by Terraform (ECS task roles, execution roles, GitHub Actions OIDC roles). Configuration and Verification Steps (per docs/aws-setup/README.md): Log in to the AWS Management Console with administrative privileges (Root or Admin). Open IAM Policies and create policy nutrition-boundary pasting docs/aws-setup/nutrition-boundary-policy.json. Verify that Access Analyzer reports zero validation errors. Open IAM Identity Center → Permission sets: Create permission set nutrition-plan attaching AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess. Create permission set nutrition-apply attaching ReadOnlyAccess and pasting docs/aws-setup/nutrition-apply-policy.json into the Inline Policy. Set session duration to 4 hours. Assign both permission sets to your designated IAM Identity Center user on the target AWS account. Verify regional isolation constraints: Core services are restricted to ap-southeast-1 (Singapore); CloudFront is global and S3 is restricted to nutrition-* buckets; an exception in ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) is granted exclusively for Amazon Bedrock and Guardrails. Security Notice: Never attach unrestricted AdministratorAccess. The project enforces an IAM Permission Boundary to cap maximum permissions and prevent unintended privilege escalation. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/iam-permission-sets.png Figure 5.2.1. Permission Sets in AWS IAM Identity Center Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.1. Permission Sets in AWS IAM Identity Center: Configuration of nutrition-plan and nutrition-apply permission sets in Identity Center. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/iam-permission-boundary.png Figure 5.2.2. IAM Permission Boundary for Project Roles Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.2. IAM Permission Boundary for Project Roles: The nutrition-boundary policy bounding maximum permissions for application roles. 5.2.3. AWS CLI SSO Login Authenticate your AWS CLI session using the pre-configured SSO session name nutrition: PowerShellCopy aws sso login --sso-session nutrition After completing browser authentication, verify your active identity with profile nutrition-plan: PowerShellCopy aws sts get-caller-identity --profile nutrition-plan Expected Output: The command responds with a valid JSON document containing UserId, Account, and Arn corresponding to your permission set. (For security reasons, actual Account IDs and sensitive data are sanitized and omitted from public documentation). Troubleshooting InvalidGrantException: This error indicates an expired SSO token session. Re-authenticate by executing aws sso login --sso-session nutrition to obtain a fresh token. 5.2.4. Bootstrap Terraform Backend on S3 Terraform State preserves the current state of AWS infrastructure managed by Terraform. The project uses Amazon S3 as a Remote Backend with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 AES256), Versioning enabled, and native state locking via use_lockfile = true (introduced in Terraform 1.10+, eliminating the need for a DynamoDB table). Follow the step-by-step instructions from infra/README.md: 1 Initialize Terraform Bootstrap Navigate to the bootstrap directory and download required providers:
PowerShellCopy terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap init 2 Review Terraform Plan Set the owner variable and save the binary execution plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:TF_VAR_owner = "your-name" terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap plan -out=tfplan Review the planned resources carefully to confirm that only intended S3 state bucket components will be created before proceeding to apply. 3 Deploy Bootstrap Switch to the nutrition-apply profile and apply the saved plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-apply" terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap apply tfplan 4 Retrieve State Bucket Name Query the created S3 state bucket name from Terraform output:
PowerShellCopy terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap output state_bucket The output displays a unique bucket name formatted as: nutrition-dev-tfstate-<account-id>.
5 Configure Dev Environment Backend Copy the backend template file from the dev environment folder and populate the bucket name:
PowerShellCopy cp infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl.example infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl Configured content inside infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl:
HCLCopy bucket = "nutrition-dev-tfstate-<account-id>" Key S3 Remote Backend Features: Terraform State is stored securely with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 AES256) and TLS enforcement. use_lockfile = true provides robust native state locking directly on S3 objects, preventing concurrent write collisions. The bucket is protected by prevent_destroy = true in the bootstrap definition to guard against accidental removal. AWS Budgets Advisory: Prior to deploying chargeable resources, learners should configure budget alert thresholds in AWS Budgets. The team project adheres to a 100 USD benchmark limit. Detailed step-by-step setup, email alerts, and screenshot evidence are covered in Module 5.6 – Monitoring, Security & Cost. Note that the bootstrap module does not automatically create AWS Budgets. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/terraform-state-s3.png Figure 5.2.3. Amazon S3 Bucket for Terraform State Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.3. Amazon S3 Bucket for Terraform State: S3 bucket nutrition-dev-tfstate with SSE-S3 encryption and use_lockfile native locking. 5.2.5. Results Verification Verify the following checklist before proceeding to infrastructure provisioning: ✓ AWS CLI successfully authenticated via SSO with return exit code 0. ✓ Profiles nutrition-plan and nutrition-apply configured correctly in AWS config. ✓ The nutrition-boundary policy exists and passes IAM Policy Validation. ✓ Terraform Bootstrap initialized and applied without permission errors. ✓ S3 Remote State bucket created in Singapore (ap-southeast-1) with encryption and public access blocks. ✓ Configuration in infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl correctly matches the actual state bucket name. ✓ No sensitive access keys or real account IDs are committed to version control. 5.2.6. Common Errors & Troubleshooting Expired AWS SSO Session (InvalidGrantException / ExpiredToken): Re-authenticate by running aws sso login --sso-session nutrition to refresh your temporary session token. Terraform State Lock: If state locking errors occur due to an aborted execution, verify that no other terraform processes are active. Only execute terraform force-unlock <LOCK-ID> after ensuring safety and proper permissions. Never manually delete the state bucket or state file. Insufficient AWS Permissions (AccessDeniedException): Check your current active profile via $env:AWS_PROFILE to ensure it is set to nutrition-apply. Compare the missing permissions against docs/aws-setup/README.md; never grant full AdministratorAccess as a workaround. ← 5.1 Workshop Overview 5.3 Core Infrastructure → 5.3 – Core Infrastructure This hands-on lab guides you through provisioning the VPC network, Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database, and Amazon Cognito authentication service using Terraform. These components provide the foundational infrastructure required for deploying the Spring Boot backend in subsequent steps. 5.3.1. VPC Networking A. Learning Objectives Deploy segmented network infrastructure for backend services and databases, ensuring Application Load Balancer (ALB), ECS Fargate, and RDS operate within appropriate network boundaries while eliminating NAT Gateway costs. B. Network Architecture According to project architectural decisions (D15 & D19), the network comprises: One VPC in Singapore (ap-southeast-1), with default CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 spanned across 2 Availability Zones. Two Public Subnets (10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24) hosting the ALB and ECS Fargate container tasks. Two Private Database Subnets (10.0.100.0/24 and 10.0.101.0/24) dedicated to Amazon RDS with zero direct Internet routing. An Internet Gateway (IGW) attached to the VPC. Route Tables: Public route table directs 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW; database route table restricts traffic strictly to internal VPC CIDRs. S3 Gateway Endpoint: Enables ECS tasks to transfer product media with Amazon S3 over AWS internal network at zero hourly cost, bypassing the Internet Gateway. CloudFront Origin-Facing Managed Prefix List: Restricts ALB ingress exclusively to CloudFront CDN origin-facing IP ranges. Three-Tier Security Group Isolation: ALB Security Group (nutrition-dev-alb): Ingress accepts HTTP (port 80) only from CloudFront Managed Prefix List; Egress forwards traffic only to ECS tasks on port 8080. ECS Security Group (nutrition-dev-ecs): Ingress accepts application traffic (port 8080) only from ALB SG; Egress allows port 5432 to RDS SG and HTTPS (port 443) outbound to AWS APIs (ECR, Bedrock, Cognito JWKS, CloudWatch). RDS Security Group (nutrition-dev-rds): Ingress permits PostgreSQL traffic (port 5432) strictly from ECS SG; direct Internet ingress is completely forbidden. C. Step-by-Step Implementation 1 Review Terraform Network Configuration Inspect infra/modules/network/main.tf to review CloudFront prefix list and S3 gateway endpoint definitions:
HCLCopy data "aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list" "cloudfront" { name = "com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing" } This ensures ALB only accepts incoming requests originating from CloudFront edge distributions.
2 Review Terraform Variables Verify parameters passed into module network from infra/envs/dev/main.tf:
name_prefix = "nutrition-dev": Unified naming prefix. enable_nat = false: Disables NAT Gateway by default to prevent hourly billing (~$32/month). ECS tasks assign public IPs in public subnets to communicate outbound with AWS APIs. 3 Generate and Review Terraform Plan Authenticate with profile nutrition-plan and generate an execution plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-plan" terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev init terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev plan -var="app_running=false" -out=tfplan Review the staged resources: 1 VPC, 4 Subnets, 1 Internet Gateway, 2 Route Tables, 3 Security Groups, and 1 S3 Gateway Endpoint. 4 Apply Core Infrastructure Switch to profile nutrition-apply and apply the plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-apply" terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev apply tfplan Architecture Note: The dev root module simultaneously provisions network, RDS, and Cognito in an idle state (app_running = false). Do not use -target flags as this can disrupt Terraform state dependency graphs. 5 Verify Resources in AWS Console Sign in to AWS Console and navigate to VPC → Your VPCs:
Confirm VPC nutrition-dev-vpc exists with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Confirm 2 Public Subnets and 2 Private DB Subnets across 2 Availability Zones. Confirm Internet Gateway attached to the VPC. Verify DB route table contains no routes toward 0.0.0.0/0. Verify the 3 Security Groups: nutrition-dev-alb, nutrition-dev-ecs, and nutrition-dev-rds. Confirm S3 Gateway Endpoint status is Available. D. Evidence Screenshots Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/vpc-resource-map.png Figure 5.3.1.1. VPC Resource Map Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.1.1. VPC Resource Map: AWS VPC console displaying VPC CIDR, subnets, and routing table associations. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/vpc-security-groups.png Figure 5.3.1.2. System Security Groups Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.1.2. System Security Groups: Ingress and egress rules for ALB, ECS, and RDS security groups. E. Results Verification ✓ VPC and subnets deployed across 2 Availability Zones. ✓ ALB and ECS enforce proper security group isolation and designated ports. ✓ RDS allows PostgreSQL connections exclusively from ECS tasks. ✓ Route tables strictly separate public and database tiers. ✓ S3 Gateway Endpoint status is Available. F. Security Notice Never include real AWS Account IDs, sensitive IPs, or internal secrets in public documentation or screenshots. 5.3.2. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Database A. Learning Objectives Provision PostgreSQL 17 on Amazon RDS, enforce zero public exposure, and automate database schema evolution using Flyway migrations. B. Database Specifications Amazon RDS PostgreSQL configuration parameters in the dev environment: Property Configured Value Service Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (Engine version 17.x) Instance Class db.t4g.micro (AWS Graviton2 ARM architecture, cost-optimized) Storage 20 GB gp3 (Autoscaling up to 100 GB) Availability Single-AZ (default for demo savings, supports Multi-AZ via rds_multi_az) Subnet Group Private database subnets (nutrition-dev-db) Public Access Disabled (publicly_accessible = false) Encryption Enabled with AWS KMS (storage_encrypted = true) Credential Management AWS Secrets Manager managed password (manage_master_user_password = true) Schema Migration Flyway migrations V1–V11 executed by Spring Boot Key Security Properties: RDS cannot be reached from the Internet, preventing public exposure and credential attacks. Security Group accepts inbound traffic on PostgreSQL port (5432) exclusively from nutrition-dev-ecs tasks. Master password is generated and rotated automatically by Secrets Manager, never stored as plaintext in code or tfstate. Flyway guarantees deterministic, versioned schema state. C. Step-by-Step Implementation 1 Review Terraform RDS Module Inspect infra/modules/rds/main.tf for essential security directives:
HCLCopy manage_master_user_password = true db_subnet_group_name = aws_db_subnet_group.main.name vpc_security_group_ids = [var.security_group_id] publicly_accessible = false multi_az = var.multi_az
manage_master_user_password = true delegates database credentials to Secrets Manager directly.
2 Verify DB Subnet Group and Security Group Ensure aws_db_subnet_group.main binds the 2 private DB subnets and attaches the RDS security group from the network module.
3 Deploy via Terraform RDS PostgreSQL was provisioned during the root apply step in Lab 5.3.1. Initialization typically takes 5–8 minutes.
4 Inspect RDS in AWS Console Navigate to Amazon RDS → Databases and select nutrition-dev-postgres:
Status: Available (when app is running) or Stopped (during idle demo periods). Engine version: PostgreSQL 17.x. Instance: db.t4g.micro | Storage: 20 GB gp3. Multi-AZ: No (Single-AZ). Public access: No. Security Group: nutrition-dev-rds. 5 Verify Secrets Manager Metadata Navigate to AWS Secrets Manager and verify the managed secret matching rds!db-.... Do not open or reveal the plaintext secret value.
6 Review Flyway Migration Structure Inspect backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/ for SQL migration files V1 through V11:
V1__catalog.sql: Categories, products, and allergens tables. V3__commerce.sql: Orders, order items, and shopping cart tables. V4__chat_usage.sql: Chatbot usage limits table. V5__product_images.sql: Product image S3 keys. V6–V8: Expanded allergens and Vietnamese unaccent search. V9__payments.sql: Payment transaction entities. V10__payment_events.sql: Idempotent payment webhook events. V11__nutrition_profiles.sql: Personalized user nutrition profiles. When backend tasks launch on ECS, Flyway reads flyway_schema_history and automatically applies pending migrations.
D. Evidence Screenshots Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/rds-configuration.png Figure 5.3.2.1. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Configuration Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.2.1. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Configuration: RDS dashboard displaying PostgreSQL 17, db.t4g.micro instance class, and encryption status. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/rds-connectivity.png Figure 5.3.2.2. RDS Connectivity & Security Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.2.2. RDS Connectivity & Security: Private subnet group binding, security group isolation, and disabled public accessibility. E. Results Verification ✓ RDS PostgreSQL 17 provisioned with instance class db.t4g.micro. ✓ Public access is disabled. ✓ Storage encryption with AWS KMS is active. ✓ Port 5432 ingress permitted strictly from ECS security group. ✓ Flyway migrations ready to execute upon application startup. F. Common Issues & Operational Runbook Terraform cannot resume stopped RDS instances: The AWS RDS API prevents Terraform from transitioning an instance from stopped to available during standard apply calls. Operational Solution (per docs/runbook.md): Use the automated lifecycle script: PowerShellCopy powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .scriptsdemo-infra.ps1 up The script invokes AWS CLI to start the RDS instance, awaits Available state, and then invokes Terraform apply. 5.3.3. Amazon Cognito Authentication A. Learning Objectives Provision a centralized user authentication system, issue JWT tokens, and enforce Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). B. Cognito Architecture According to system security architecture: User Pool (nutrition-dev-users): Email-based user identification, automated verification email dispatch, and strong password enforcement (8+ chars, uppercase, lowercase, numbers, symbols). App Client (nutrition-dev-spa): Designed for Single Page Applications (React SPA) with generate_secret = false because browser clients cannot securely hold secret keys. Authentication Flows: Utilizes Secure Remote Password protocol (ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH) and refresh tokens (ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH). Does not use Cognito Hosted UI, opting for embedded React authentication screens. User Groups: Two pre-configured groups: USER (customers) and ADMIN (store administrators). Backend JWT Verification: Spring Boot Resource Server verifies JWT cryptographic signatures against Cognito JWKS, extracting user identity from claim sub and authorities from claim cognito:groups. C. Step-by-Step Implementation 1 Review Cognito Terraform Module Inspect infra/modules/cognito/main.tf for User Pool, App Client, and recovery settings:
HCLCopy resource "aws_cognito_user_pool_client" "spa" { name = "${var.name_prefix}-spa" user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.users.id generate_secret = false explicit_auth_flows = [ “ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH”, “ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH”, “ALLOW_ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH”, ] }
2 Review USER and ADMIN User Groups Verify user group definitions in infra/modules/cognito/main.tf:
HCLCopy resource "aws_cognito_user_group" "admin" { name = "ADMIN" user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.users.id } resource “aws_cognito_user_group” “user” { name = “USER” user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.users.id }
Registered users belong to USER. Only users assigned to ADMIN are granted access to administrative order and catalog endpoints.
3 Deploy Cognito Module Cognito is managed as code and provisioned during the root apply step. Do not manually create user pools in the AWS Console to avoid state drift.
4 Inspect Cognito in AWS Console Navigate to Amazon Cognito → User pools and select nutrition-dev-users:
Verify User Pool ID prefix: ap-southeast-1_.... Under App integration → App clients: Verify client nutrition-dev-spa with No client secret. Under Groups: Verify ADMIN and USER groups exist. 5 Verify API Authorization Enforcement (per docs/demo.md) Verify backend Spring Boot RBAC enforcement against incoming API calls:
Unauthenticated Requests: Calling protected endpoints without an Authorization: Bearer <token> header responds with HTTP 401 Unauthorized. Standard User accessing Admin API: A user in group USER attempting to access /api/admin/** triggers a claim inspection on cognito:groups and responds with HTTP 403 Forbidden. Admin User: Validated successfully and granted administrative permissions. D. Evidence Screenshots Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/cognito-user-groups.png Figure 5.3.3.1. USER and ADMIN Groups in Amazon Cognito Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.3.1. USER and ADMIN Groups in Amazon Cognito: AWS Cognito console displaying configured user pool groups. E. Results Verification ✓ Cognito User Pool and SPA Client provisioned. ✓ Client Secret disabled for browser client security. ✓ USER and ADMIN groups created. ✓ JWT tokens validated by backend with HTTP 401 / 403 access control. ← 5.2 Prerequisites 5.4 App Deployment → 5.4 – Application Deployment 1. Learning Objectives Package Spring Boot 4 into an ARM64-optimized Docker container image. Authenticate with Amazon ECR and push the backend container image. Deploy the ECS Fargate service with 1 active task wired to the ALB. Compile the React 19 frontend and synchronize assets to Amazon S3 / CloudFront. 2. Prerequisites Completed Lab 5.3 (infrastructure outputs available).
3. Step-by-Step Practical Steps 1 Package Spring Boot Backend & Push to ECR Compile the JAR file and build the linux/arm64 Docker image:
TerminalCopy # 1. Build JAR package cd backend ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests 2. Extract ECR URL cd ../infra/envs/dev ECR_URL=$(terraform output -raw ecr_repository_url) cd ../../../backend
3. Authenticate Docker with ECR aws ecr get-login-password –region ap-southeast-1 | docker login –username AWS –password-stdin $ECR_URL
4. Build ARM64 Docker container image docker build –platform linux/arm64 -t $ECR_URL:latest .
5. Push image to Amazon ECR docker push $ECR_URL:latest
2 Start ECS Service & Launch Active Task Apply Terraform with app_running=true to spin up the ALB and ECS Fargate task:
TerminalCopy cd ../infra/envs/dev terraform apply -var="app_running=true" -var="api_desired_count=1" -auto-approve 3 Build & Deploy React Frontend to S3 Build the React SPA bundle and invalidate the CloudFront edge cache:
TerminalCopy cd ../../../frontend npm install npm run build cd ../infra/envs/dev FRONTEND_BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw frontend_bucket_name) DIST_ID=$(terraform output -raw cloudfront_distribution_id) cd ../../../frontend
aws s3 sync dist/ s3://$FRONTEND_BUCKET/ –delete aws cloudfront create-invalidation –distribution-id $DIST_ID –paths “/*"
Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.4-deployment/ecr-image-push.png Backend Image Pushed to Amazon ECR Evidence screenshot will be updated. Backend Image Pushed to Amazon ECR: ECR Console displaying the pushed container image with latest tag and scan results. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.4-deployment/ecs-task-running.png ECS Fargate Task in RUNNING State Evidence screenshot will be updated. ECS Fargate Task in RUNNING State: ECS Console displaying 1 healthy running container task in nutrition-dev-cluster. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.4-deployment/cloudfront-app-live.png Live Application on CloudFront Domain Evidence screenshot will be updated. Live Application on CloudFront Domain: Browser viewing the live React e-commerce application with 152 USDA products. 4. Verification & Expected Output Navigating to https://<cloudfront_domain>/ displays the storefront. Backend Actuator health check returns healthy: Health CheckCopy curl -s https:///api/actuator/health # Returns: {"status":"UP"} 5. Common Errors & Troubleshooting Login Denied on ECR: The ECR authorization token expires after 12 hours. Refresh token via aws ecr get-login-password. ECS Task Exits with Crash: Check CloudWatch Log Group /ecs/nutrition-dev-backend for database connectivity issues. ← 5.3 Core Infra 5.5 Bedrock AI → 5.5 – Amazon Bedrock Integration 1. Learning Objectives Request model access for Amazon Nova 2 Lite in Tokyo (ap-northeast-1). Configure Bedrock Guardrails to mitigate prompt injection and medical diagnostic queries. Validate the end-to-end AI intent parsing and PostgreSQL SQL lookup workflow. 2. Prerequisites Completed Lab 5.4. Active AWS credentials with Bedrock access in Asia Pacific (Tokyo).
3. Step-by-Step Practical Steps 1 Enable Model Access in Tokyo (ap-northeast-1) In the AWS Management Console, switch your region to Tokyo (ap-northeast-1):
Open Amazon Bedrock → Click Model access. Click Modify model access. Locate provider Amazon and select Amazon Nova 2 Lite (or inference profile jp.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0). Click Next and Submit to finalize access approval. 2 Configure Guardrails via Terraform Verify Guardrail variables in infra/envs/dev/terraform.tfvars:
terraform.tfvarsCopy bedrock_region = "ap-northeast-1" bedrock_model_id = "amazon.nova-lite-v1:0" bedrock_inference_profile_id = "jp.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0" guardrail_tier = "STANDARD" 3 Test AI Nutrition Intent Query API Execute a test cURL request to verify conversational parameter extraction:
TerminalCopy curl -X POST "https:///api/ai/nutrition-lookup" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "find dinner under 450 calories with over 30g protein and gluten free"}' Expected JSON response containing verified USDA food items matching criteria:
Response JSONCopy { "intent": "FIND_FOOD", "extractedFilters": { "maxCalories": 450, "minProtein": 30, "excludedAllergens": ["GLUTEN"] }, "products": [ { "id": 18, "name": "Grilled Chicken Breast with Steamed Asparagus", "calories": 310, "protein": 36.5, "carbohydrates": 3.8, "fat": 4.5, "allergens": [] } ] } Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.5-bedrock/bedrock-model-access.png Amazon Nova 2 Lite Model Access in Tokyo Evidence screenshot will be updated. Amazon Nova 2 Lite Model Access in Tokyo: AWS Bedrock Console displaying Access granted for Amazon Nova 2 Lite. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.5-bedrock/bedrock-guardrail.png Bedrock Guardrail Safety Filters Configuration Evidence screenshot will be updated. Bedrock Guardrail Safety Filters Configuration: Bedrock Guardrails Console displaying content filtering and topic deny policies. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.5-bedrock/ai-lookup-test.png AI Nutrition Lookup API Response Evidence screenshot will be updated. AI Nutrition Lookup API Response: Terminal / Postman screenshot displaying the structured JSON payload. 4. Verification & Expected Output AI extracts search parameters cleanly; backend returns verified PostgreSQL items; clinical advice queries are intercepted by Guardrails.
5. Common Errors & Troubleshooting AccessDeniedException: Model access was not granted in Tokyo (ap-northeast-1). Request model access in the Bedrock Console. ← 5.4 App Deployment 5.6 Monitoring & Cost → 5.6 – Monitoring, Security & Cost Management 1. Learning Objectives Stream and inspect live container logs with Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure metric alarms and email notifications via Amazon SNS. Enforce budget guardrails using AWS Budgets ($10 threshold). Operate the demo lifecycle script demo-infra.ps1 and reconcile empirical costs from AWS Cost Explorer. 2. Prerequisites Completed Lab 5.5. Live application on AWS.
3. Step-by-Step Practical Steps 1 Configure Alert Email for CloudWatch & Budgets Set your notification email and apply Terraform configuration:
TerminalCopy cd infra/envs/dev export TF_VAR_alert_email="your-email@example.com" terraform apply -auto-approve Check your email inbox for "AWS Notification - Subscription Confirmation" and click Confirm subscription.
2 Inspect Real-Time CloudWatch Logs Tail live container logs from your terminal:
TerminalCopy aws logs tail /ecs/nutrition-dev-backend --follow --region ap-southeast-1 3 Operate the Automated Demo Lifecycle Script Control active compute costs using the demo script:
PowerShellCopy # Before presentation (~10-15 mins): Spin up RDS & ECS tasks powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .scriptsdemo-infra.ps1 up After presentation (~5-10 mins): Stop RDS & destroy ECS tasks to cease hourly compute fees powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .scriptsdemo-infra.ps1 down
4 Empirical AWS Cost Explorer Spending Summary Active development spend from Nov 01 to Nov 21, 2026:
AWS Service Actual Cost (USD) Operational Notes Amazon RDS PostgreSQL (db.t4g.micro) 2.77 Instance hours during demo + 20 GB gp3 storage. Application Load Balancer (ALB) 1.29 Active load balancer hours during integration testing. Amazon ECS Fargate (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB RAM) 1.21 Serverless container compute runtime. Public IPv4 Address 0.74 Public IPv4 allocation fees for task in public subnet. Amazon Bedrock (Nova 2 Lite) 0.21 Token usage for conversational intent extraction. AWS Secrets Manager 0.20 Encrypted credential vault storage and lookups. Total Actual Spend 6.44 100% Offset by Promotional AWS Credits Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.6-monitoring/cloudwatch-logs.png Real-Time CloudWatch Logs Inspection Evidence screenshot will be updated. Real-Time CloudWatch Logs Inspection: CloudWatch Logs stream recording HTTP 200 responses. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.6-monitoring/cloudwatch-alarms.png CloudWatch Alarms Dashboard Status Evidence screenshot will be updated. CloudWatch Alarms Dashboard Status: CloudWatch Alarms dashboard displaying all metrics in healthy OK status. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.6-monitoring/aws-budgets.png AWS Budgets & Cost Explorer Reconciled Evidence screenshot will be updated. AWS Budgets & Cost Explorer Reconciled: AWS Budgets dashboard showing $6.44 spend well within the $10 budget ceiling. 4. Verification & Expected Output Alarms indicate OK; email notification received; demo script successfully starts and halts running compute on demand.
5. Common Errors & Troubleshooting AWS Automatically Restarts Stopped RDS After 7 Days: AWS automatically starts stopped DB instances after 7 days. Re-run demo-infra.ps1 down if not presenting. ← 5.5 Bedrock AI 5.7 Clean-up → 5.7 – Resource Cleanup & Teardown 1. Learning Objectives Master the complete, safe, and dependency-ordered infrastructure teardown procedure. Purge S3 buckets, RDS database, ECS service, ECR images, and Cognito User Pool upon course completion. Validate on the AWS Console that zero active billable resources remain. 2. Prerequisites All final project report artifacts, screenshots, and evaluations have been safely exported.
3. Step-by-Step Practical Steps 1 Final Database Snapshot (Optional) Preserve database records for future reference:
TerminalCopy aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier nutrition-dev-postgres --db-snapshot-identifier nutrition-dev-final-backup --region ap-southeast-1 2 Empty Private S3 Buckets AWS prevents deletion of non-empty buckets. Purge all bucket contents:
TerminalCopy cd infra/envs/dev FRONTEND_BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw frontend_bucket_name) IMAGES_BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw images_bucket_name) aws s3 rm s3://$FRONTEND_BUCKET/ –recursive aws s3 rm s3://$IMAGES_BUCKET/ –recursive
3 Destroy Dev Infrastructure with Terraform Destroy all cloud infrastructure provisioned in the dev environment:
TerminalCopy terraform destroy -auto-approve 4 Destroy Bootstrap State Storage Purge and destroy the bootstrap S3 remote state bucket:
TerminalCopy cd ../bootstrap TF_STATE_BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw state_bucket_name) aws s3 rm s3://$TF_STATE_BUCKET/ --recursive terraform destroy -auto-approve 5 Validate Resource Deletion in AWS Console Check each service in Singapore (ap-southeast-1):
ECS: Zero active clusters or tasks. RDS: Zero databases (only manual snapshot if created). EC2 / VPC: Load Balancers and Target Groups deleted; zero unattached Elastic IPs. CloudFront: Distribution disabled and removed. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.7-cleanup/terraform-destroy-success.png Terraform Destroy Completion Evidence screenshot will be updated. Terraform Destroy Completion: Terminal displaying "Destroy complete! Resources: XX destroyed". Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.7-cleanup/console-clean-verification.png AWS Console Post-Cleanup Verification Evidence screenshot will be updated. AWS Console Post-Cleanup Verification: RDS and ECS Consoles confirming 0 active resources. 4. Verification & Expected Output terraform destroy exits with code 0; AWS Console reflects zero lingering resources; AWS Cost Explorer flatlines to $0.00.
5. Common Errors & Troubleshooting RDS Deletion Protection Enabled: In infra/modules/rds/main.tf set deletion_protection = false, apply, then re-run destroy. ← 5.6 Monitoring & Cost

title: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam
content:
Events Participated / Event 2 - Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam ← Back to Events EVENT HARVEST REPORT Cloud Computing & Artificial Intelligence Official • AWS Community FIRESIDE CHAT WITH DR. WERNER VOGELS Engineering at Scale, the Renaissance Developer, and the Future of Artificial Intelligence
Event Name: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Event Date: Friday, October 2, 2026 Date & Time: 08:30 AM – 12:00 PM, October 2, 2026 (UTC+7) Location / Format: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels (Vice President & CTO, Amazon.com) Role: Attendee Photo 1: Group photo from the Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels – Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam, October 2, 2026. 01 1. Event Information Event Name: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Event Date: Friday, October 2, 2026 Date & Time: 08:30 AM – 12:00 PM, October 2, 2026 (UTC+7) Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels Speaker Position: Vice President and Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon.com Participation Role: Attendee Event Location / Participation Format: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Event Video: Watch on YouTube 02 2. Event Objectives The Fireside Chat aimed to provide insights into the future of cloud computing and artificial intelligence in Vietnam.
The main objectives included:
Exploring the future of AWS Cloud and AI adoption in Vietnam. Understanding engineering principles for building reliable systems at scale. Discovering how AI is transforming application development and software engineering. Learning about the evolving responsibilities of developers in the AI era. Developing a broader engineering mindset through the experiences of AWS technology leadership. 03 3. Speaker Dr. Werner Vogels Vice President and Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon.com
Dr. Werner Vogels is a technology leader known for his experience in cloud computing, distributed systems, and large-scale software architectures.
During the discussion, he shared perspectives on the development of AWS, engineering at scale, and the future of software development in an AI-driven world.
His insights emphasized the continuing importance of engineering fundamentals, technical judgment, and lifelong learning.
04 4. Key Highlights 4.1. The Origins and Evolution of AWS The discussion explored the origins of Amazon Web Services and its evolution into a major cloud computing platform.
Key points included:
The early thinking behind developing cloud infrastructure. Building cloud services that support different customer needs. Designing systems that can grow from small applications to global-scale workloads. Using customer requirements to guide technology decisions. This topic highlighted how cloud computing enables organizations to access scalable infrastructure without building every component themselves.
4.2. Engineering at Scale Another major theme was the challenge of designing and operating systems serving large numbers of users.
Important engineering considerations included:
Scalability and workload growth. Reliability and service availability. Automation and operational efficiency. Resilient system design. Monitoring and long-term maintainability. The discussion emphasized that successful software engineering involves more than building features. Systems must also remain dependable as their complexity and usage increase.
4.3. The Renaissance Developer Dr. Werner Vogels introduced the concept of the Renaissance Developer, describing how software engineers must adapt as AI tools become more capable.
Modern developers need to develop skills beyond writing source code.
They should also understand system architecture, solve complex problems, communicate effectively, and evaluate technical decisions.
AI assistants can support everyday development activities, but human knowledge and responsibility remain essential.
4.4. AI, Prototyping, and Engineering Responsibility Artificial intelligence can significantly accelerate the process of turning ideas into working prototypes.
AI tools may help developers generate initial code, explore solutions, and automate repetitive tasks.
However, faster development does not automatically guarantee software quality.
Developers must still:
Review AI-generated code. Validate application behavior. Test important functionalities. Identify security and reliability risks. Make informed architectural decisions. The discussion reinforced the idea that AI should support engineering expertise rather than replace it.
05 5. Key Learnings 5.1. Engineering Mindset and Architecture Scalability-first thinking: Developers should consider how their systems might evolve as application requirements and workloads change. Scalability is important, but the chosen architecture should remain appropriate to actual project needs. Prototyping mindset: AI tools can help teams evaluate ideas quickly and experiment with different approaches. Before deployment, prototypes still require testing, refinement, and technical validation. Engineering fundamentals: Core knowledge of programming, system architecture, distributed systems, and problem-solving remains valuable even as development tools evolve. 5.2. The Evolution of Software Development The discussion helped me better understand the changing role of software engineers.
Developers are increasingly expected to combine coding skills with architecture, analytical thinking, and the ability to work effectively with AI assistants.
AI can reduce repetitive work, allowing developers to devote more attention to technical challenges and software quality.
Continuous learning is essential to staying current with cloud computing and AI technologies.
5.3. Practical Applications Integrating AI into development workflows: AI assistants can support coding, documentation, code review, testing preparation, and rapid prototyping. Their results still require human validation. Improving system design: Engineering-at-scale principles can guide decisions about reliability, deployment, monitoring, and scalability in individual or group projects. Strengthening self-learning: The session encouraged proactive learning through AWS documentation, practical projects, and programs such as First Cloud AI Journey. 5.4. Application to Nutrition E-Commerce The ideas discussed in the Fireside Chat are relevant to the Nutrition E-Commerce group project:
Cloud architecture: Reviewing the roles of Amazon ECS Fargate, Application Load Balancer, Amazon RDS, and Amazon CloudFront in the overall system design. AI integration: Considering how Amazon Bedrock can support application features while maintaining appropriate validation and security controls. Software reliability: Understanding the importance of testing, deployment verification, and monitoring before considering an application ready for users. Development productivity: Exploring how AI-assisted development can help with prototyping and documentation without replacing human technical judgment. These points describe how the session's concepts relate to the project. They do not imply that every technology was personally implemented during the event.
06 6. Event Experience and Personal Reflection Attending the Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels was a valuable opportunity to explore the future of cloud computing and artificial intelligence from the perspective of an experienced technology leader.
Two ideas stood out to me:
Learning from technology leadership: The discussion provided a broader perspective on the principles behind cloud platforms and the challenges of building reliable systems at scale. Understanding the Renaissance Developer: I gained a clearer understanding that modern developers need more than programming knowledge. They must develop systems thinking, communication skills, technical judgment, and the ability to learn continuously. “AI can make software development faster, but developers remain responsible for the quality, security, and reliability of their solutions.” This experience strengthened my motivation to continue learning AWS Cloud, application architecture, and AI technologies throughout my First Cloud AI Journey.
#AWS #WernerVogels #FiresideChat #CloudAI #RenaissanceDeveloper #EngineeringAtScale #FirstCloudAIJourney ← Back to Events ↑ Back to top

title: AWS Event-Driven Architecture
content:
← Back to Articles AWS / Distributed Systems / Architecture AWS EVENT-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURE – WHEN ALL SERVICES SUCCEED, WHY CAN DATA STILL BE WRONG? View post on AWS Study Group VN community 04/11/2026 AWS Event-Driven Architecture – Event Processing, Ordering and Atomic Publishing While researching Event-Driven Architecture on AWS, I identified a critical paradox: A system can process all events with 100% success yet still generate incorrect business data due to Race Conditions. This stems directly from the asynchronous nature of decoupled services, particularly when orchestrating Amazon S3, EventBridge, SQS, AWS Lambda, and DynamoDB.
1. WHAT IS THE PROBLEM HERE? Amazon S3 Event Notifications operate on an At-Least-Once Delivery model, providing no inherent guarantee that events arrive exactly once or in chronological order.
Suppose an AI document processing pipeline updates a file from Version A to Version B:
Lambda A: Processes baseline Version A in 15 seconds.Lambda B: Processes updated Version B in only 4 seconds.Outcome: B completes first, but Lambda A finishes later and overwrites the newer result with stale data. Both Lambda invocations succeed with HTTP 200, yet the final persisted business outcome is completely corrupted.
Worker / InvocationDocument VersionStart TimeDurationWrite TimeActual Outcome Worker AVersion A (v1)T015 secondsT0 + 15sOverwrites newer result of B Worker BVersion B (v2 - Latest)T0 + 2s4 secondsT0 + 6sOverwritten by stale output from A Core reality: Every individual AWS service worked as designed, yet the business result became corrupted due to uneven invocation latency across distributed workers. 2. WHY ARE IDEMPOTENCY AND SQS NOT ENOUGH? Engineers commonly assume that applying Idempotency and SQS FIFO queues will eliminate race conditions in event-driven systems. In practice, both exhibit fundamental boundaries:
Idempotency: Prevents duplicate side-effects from identical event retries, but cannot prevent an older stale event from overwriting a newer result.Amazon SQS FIFO: Enforces strict ordering within Message Groups, but cannot restore chronological order if events were already delivered out-of-order prior to entering the queue.TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use): Even when a Lambda inspects object versions before processing, underlying data can change during execution. 3. PROPOSED ARCHITECTURAL SOLUTION Rather than allowing Lambda functions to directly overwrite shared storage, the recommended pattern blends five core mechanisms:
S3 Versioning: Retrieve the exact input data version. Guarantees workers read the specific object version tied to the event.S3 Sequencer: Determine event sequence order on the same object key using the physical hexadecimal timestamp in S3 event payloads.Immutable Output: Each Lambda writes results to a dedicated immutable path (e.g., output/{key}/{version_id}/result.json), preventing direct overwrite conflicts.DynamoDB Conditional Write: Control result publishing using atomic Compare-and-Swap conditional updates. Only updates state if the sequencer is newer.Reconciliation: Recover interrupted tasks and reconcile state inconsistencies when partial failures occur. ComponentRole in ArchitectureCorrectness Guarantee Mechanism Amazon S3 VersioningInput source data preservationImmutable Version ID per PutObject invocation S3 Object SequencerOriginal event ordering authorityHexadecimal string reflecting physical S3 commit order Immutable OutputIsolated intermediate storageDedicated prefix per worker, zero direct overwrite DynamoDB Conditional WriteAtomic result pointer publishingCompare-and-Swap: updates state only if s3_sequencer is newer Reconciliation WorkerPartial failure recoveryAudits state discrepancies between S3 and DynamoDB pointer DynamoDB Atomic Conditional Update Pattern (Compare-and-Swap):
UpdateItem( Key = { "object_key": "document-123.pdf" }, UpdateExpression = "SET latest_version = :v, result_uri = :uri, s3_sequencer = :seq, updated_at = :ts", ConditionExpression = "attribute_not_exists(object_key) OR s3_sequencer < :seq", ExpressionAttributeValues = { ":seq": event.s3.object.sequencer, ":v": event.s3.object.versionId, ":uri": "s3://bucket/output/doc-123/v2/result.json", ":ts": "2026-11-04T10:30:00Z" } ) Under this architecture, Lambda A can finish after B without ever overwriting B's published result.
However, Amazon S3 and DynamoDB do not share an atomic two-phase commit transaction. Systems must incorporate Retry and Recovery mechanisms to handle partial failures when S3 writes succeed but DynamoDB updates are interrupted. 4. CONCLUSION & PRINCIPLES In cloud architecture: 100% successful Lambda invocations do not equate to 100% correct business state.
Instead of attempting to force every distributed event to process in strict serial order, architectures should control which version is permitted to publish the authoritative result.
“100% Lambda Invocations successful does not equal 100% business correctness.” Core Distributed Design Principles: 1. Decouple Processing from Publishing: Leverage Immutable Output for processing and atomic pointers for publishing.2. Enforce Ordering at the Destination: Use S3 Sequencers and DynamoDB ConditionExpression instead of fragile queue arrival order.3. Design for Partial Failure: Build Reconciliation Workers to automatically heal cross-service inconsistencies.
