Technical Workshop Guide Deploying Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS Hands-on Deployment Guide: Spring Boot 4, React 19, ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL, Bedrock AI & Terraform
A comprehensive step-by-step practical lab guide enabling engineers and students to deploy an end-to-end cloud-native nutrition e-commerce platform on Amazon Web Services. The entire infrastructure is automated via Terraform, running containerized Spring Boot 4 backend on serverless ECS Fargate, managed PostgreSQL on RDS, and generative AI intent parsing with Amazon Bedrock Nova 2 Lite. 5.1 Overview 5.2 Prerequisites 5.3 Core Infra 5.4 App Deployment 5.5 Bedrock AI 5.6 Monitoring & Cost 5.7 Clean-up 5.1. Workshop Overview Building a Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS This workshop guides you through deploying a cloud-native nutrition e-commerce platform on AWS using React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL, integrated with Amazon Bedrock for natural language food search. Learners will practice provisioning infrastructure, deploying application workloads, integrating AI capabilities, monitoring systems, and managing AWS cloud costs. Workshop Objectives Understand cloud web application architecture on AWS. Deploy frontend, backend, and managed database tiers. Integrate Amazon Bedrock for AI-assisted nutritional queries. Establish monitoring, security controls, and cost optimization. Overall Architecture Overall Architecture Diagram of Nutrition E-Commerce on AWS. The React application is distributed globally via CloudFront and S3. API requests are routed through an Application Load Balancer to Spring Boot on ECS Fargate. PostgreSQL is hosted on Amazon RDS, Cognito manages user authentication, and Amazon Bedrock powers nutritional intent extraction. Core application infrastructure is hosted in Singapore, with Bedrock and Guardrails operating in Tokyo. Workshop Roadmap 5.2. Prerequisites: Prepare AWS Account and developer toolchain. 5.3. Core Infrastructure: Provision cloud resources using Terraform. 5.4. Application Deployment: Deploy React and Spring Boot to AWS. 5.5. Amazon Bedrock: Integrate AI conversational nutrition search. 5.6. Monitoring & Cost: Configure observability, security, and budgets. 5.7. Resource Cleanup: Stop or tear down resources after the workshop. Expected Outcome Upon completing this workshop, learners will be capable of deploying, operating, and testing an AI-enabled nutrition e-commerce system on AWS while understanding how to monitor and control cloud expenditures. 5.2 Prerequisites → 5.2 – Prerequisites & Environment Setup Before deploying the Nutrition E-Commerce platform on AWS, learners must prepare an AWS account, developer toolchains, IAM access permissions, and a remote storage backend for Terraform State. This hands-on lab guides you through environment verification, configuring AWS IAM Identity Center, and bootstrapping the Terraform Backend on Amazon S3. 5.2.1. Tooling Preparation The table below lists the required developer toolchains and runtimes: Tool Requirement AWS Account Permissions to configure required AWS services (VPC, ECS, RDS, IAM, CloudFront, Bedrock) AWS CLI Version 2 (AWS CLI v2.x) Terraform Version ≥ 1.10 (tested with Terraform v1.10.5) Java JDK 21 (Eclipse Temurin or OpenJDK 21) Node.js & npm Compatible with repository (Node.js ≥ 20.x or 22.x LTS, npm ≥ 10.x) Docker Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with multi-platform container build support (linux/arm64) Git Source code version control (Git ≥ 2.40.x) PowerShell PowerShell 7 or Windows PowerShell for running verification commands and lifecycle scripts on Windows 5.2.2. Configure AWS Access & IAM Infrastructure provisioning adheres strictly to the Least Privilege principle with the following IAM components: AWS IAM Identity Center: Centrally manages user authentication and role assignments to AWS accounts via Single Sign-On (SSO). Permission set nutrition-plan: Attached with AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess, used for daily inspection, syntax validation, and planning (terraform plan). Permission set nutrition-apply: Combines ReadOnlyAccess with an inline policy from nutrition-apply-policy.json to apply approved infrastructure changes. Policy nutrition-boundary: Enforces a maximum permission boundary (nutrition-boundary-policy.json) on all IAM roles generated by Terraform (ECS task roles, execution roles, GitHub Actions OIDC roles). Configuration and Verification Steps (per docs/aws-setup/README.md): Log in to the AWS Management Console with administrative privileges (Root or Admin). Open IAM Policies and create policy nutrition-boundary pasting docs/aws-setup/nutrition-boundary-policy.json. Verify that Access Analyzer reports zero validation errors. Open IAM Identity Center → Permission sets: Create permission set nutrition-plan attaching AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess. Create permission set nutrition-apply attaching ReadOnlyAccess and pasting docs/aws-setup/nutrition-apply-policy.json into the Inline Policy. Set session duration to 4 hours. Assign both permission sets to your designated IAM Identity Center user on the target AWS account. Verify regional isolation constraints: Core services are restricted to ap-southeast-1 (Singapore); CloudFront is global and S3 is restricted to nutrition-* buckets; an exception in ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) is granted exclusively for Amazon Bedrock and Guardrails. Security Notice: Never attach unrestricted AdministratorAccess. The project enforces an IAM Permission Boundary to cap maximum permissions and prevent unintended privilege escalation. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/iam-permission-sets.png Figure 5.2.1. Permission Sets in AWS IAM Identity Center Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.1. Permission Sets in AWS IAM Identity Center: Configuration of nutrition-plan and nutrition-apply permission sets in Identity Center. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/iam-permission-boundary.png Figure 5.2.2. IAM Permission Boundary for Project Roles Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.2. IAM Permission Boundary for Project Roles: The nutrition-boundary policy bounding maximum permissions for application roles. 5.2.3. AWS CLI SSO Login Authenticate your AWS CLI session using the pre-configured SSO session name nutrition: PowerShellCopy aws sso login --sso-session nutrition After completing browser authentication, verify your active identity with profile nutrition-plan: PowerShellCopy aws sts get-caller-identity --profile nutrition-plan Expected Output: The command responds with a valid JSON document containing UserId, Account, and Arn corresponding to your permission set. (For security reasons, actual Account IDs and sensitive data are sanitized and omitted from public documentation). Troubleshooting InvalidGrantException: This error indicates an expired SSO token session. Re-authenticate by executing aws sso login --sso-session nutrition to obtain a fresh token. 5.2.4. Bootstrap Terraform Backend on S3 Terraform State preserves the current state of AWS infrastructure managed by Terraform. The project uses Amazon S3 as a Remote Backend with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 AES256), Versioning enabled, and native state locking via use_lockfile = true (introduced in Terraform 1.10+, eliminating the need for a DynamoDB table). Follow the step-by-step instructions from infra/README.md: 1 Initialize Terraform Bootstrap Navigate to the bootstrap directory and download required providers:
PowerShellCopy terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap init 2 Review Terraform Plan Set the owner variable and save the binary execution plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:TF_VAR_owner = "your-name" terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap plan -out=tfplan Review the planned resources carefully to confirm that only intended S3 state bucket components will be created before proceeding to apply. 3 Deploy Bootstrap Switch to the nutrition-apply profile and apply the saved plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-apply" terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap apply tfplan 4 Retrieve State Bucket Name Query the created S3 state bucket name from Terraform output:
PowerShellCopy terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap output state_bucket The output displays a unique bucket name formatted as: nutrition-dev-tfstate-<account-id>.
5 Configure Dev Environment Backend Copy the backend template file from the dev environment folder and populate the bucket name:
PowerShellCopy cp infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl.example infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl Configured content inside infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl:
HCLCopy bucket = "nutrition-dev-tfstate-<account-id>" Key S3 Remote Backend Features: Terraform State is stored securely with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 AES256) and TLS enforcement. use_lockfile = true provides robust native state locking directly on S3 objects, preventing concurrent write collisions. The bucket is protected by prevent_destroy = true in the bootstrap definition to guard against accidental removal. AWS Budgets Advisory: Prior to deploying chargeable resources, learners should configure budget alert thresholds in AWS Budgets. The team project adheres to a 100 USD benchmark limit. Detailed step-by-step setup, email alerts, and screenshot evidence are covered in Module 5.6 – Monitoring, Security & Cost. Note that the bootstrap module does not automatically create AWS Budgets. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/terraform-state-s3.png Figure 5.2.3. Amazon S3 Bucket for Terraform State Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.3. Amazon S3 Bucket for Terraform State: S3 bucket nutrition-dev-tfstate with SSE-S3 encryption and use_lockfile native locking. 5.2.5. Results Verification Verify the following checklist before proceeding to infrastructure provisioning: ✓ AWS CLI successfully authenticated via SSO with return exit code 0. ✓ Profiles nutrition-plan and nutrition-apply configured correctly in AWS config. ✓ The nutrition-boundary policy exists and passes IAM Policy Validation. ✓ Terraform Bootstrap initialized and applied without permission errors. ✓ S3 Remote State bucket created in Singapore (ap-southeast-1) with encryption and public access blocks. ✓ Configuration in infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl correctly matches the actual state bucket name. ✓ No sensitive access keys or real account IDs are committed to version control. 5.2.6. Common Errors & Troubleshooting Expired AWS SSO Session (InvalidGrantException / ExpiredToken): Re-authenticate by running aws sso login --sso-session nutrition to refresh your temporary session token. Terraform State Lock: If state locking errors occur due to an aborted execution, verify that no other terraform processes are active. Only execute terraform force-unlock <LOCK-ID> after ensuring safety and proper permissions. Never manually delete the state bucket or state file. Insufficient AWS Permissions (AccessDeniedException): Check your current active profile via $env:AWS_PROFILE to ensure it is set to nutrition-apply. Compare the missing permissions against docs/aws-setup/README.md; never grant full AdministratorAccess as a workaround. ← 5.1 Workshop Overview 5.3 Core Infrastructure → 5.3 – Core Infrastructure This hands-on lab guides you through provisioning the VPC network, Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database, and Amazon Cognito authentication service using Terraform. These components provide the foundational infrastructure required for deploying the Spring Boot backend in subsequent steps. 5.3.1. VPC Networking A. Learning Objectives Deploy segmented network infrastructure for backend services and databases, ensuring Application Load Balancer (ALB), ECS Fargate, and RDS operate within appropriate network boundaries while eliminating NAT Gateway costs. B. Network Architecture According to project architectural decisions (D15 & D19), the network comprises: One VPC in Singapore (ap-southeast-1), with default CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 spanned across 2 Availability Zones. Two Public Subnets (10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24) hosting the ALB and ECS Fargate container tasks. Two Private Database Subnets (10.0.100.0/24 and 10.0.101.0/24) dedicated to Amazon RDS with zero direct Internet routing. An Internet Gateway (IGW) attached to the VPC. Route Tables: Public route table directs 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW; database route table restricts traffic strictly to internal VPC CIDRs. S3 Gateway Endpoint: Enables ECS tasks to transfer product media with Amazon S3 over AWS internal network at zero hourly cost, bypassing the Internet Gateway. CloudFront Origin-Facing Managed Prefix List: Restricts ALB ingress exclusively to CloudFront CDN origin-facing IP ranges. Three-Tier Security Group Isolation: ALB Security Group (nutrition-dev-alb): Ingress accepts HTTP (port 80) only from CloudFront Managed Prefix List; Egress forwards traffic only to ECS tasks on port 8080. ECS Security Group (nutrition-dev-ecs): Ingress accepts application traffic (port 8080) only from ALB SG; Egress allows port 5432 to RDS SG and HTTPS (port 443) outbound to AWS APIs (ECR, Bedrock, Cognito JWKS, CloudWatch). RDS Security Group (nutrition-dev-rds): Ingress permits PostgreSQL traffic (port 5432) strictly from ECS SG; direct Internet ingress is completely forbidden. C. Step-by-Step Implementation 1 Review Terraform Network Configuration Inspect infra/modules/network/main.tf to review CloudFront prefix list and S3 gateway endpoint definitions:
HCLCopy data "aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list" "cloudfront" { name = "com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing" } This ensures ALB only accepts incoming requests originating from CloudFront edge distributions.
2 Review Terraform Variables Verify parameters passed into module network from infra/envs/dev/main.tf:
name_prefix = "nutrition-dev": Unified naming prefix. enable_nat = false: Disables NAT Gateway by default to prevent hourly billing (~$32/month). ECS tasks assign public IPs in public subnets to communicate outbound with AWS APIs. 3 Generate and Review Terraform Plan Authenticate with profile nutrition-plan and generate an execution plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-plan" terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev init terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev plan -var="app_running=false" -out=tfplan Review the staged resources: 1 VPC, 4 Subnets, 1 Internet Gateway, 2 Route Tables, 3 Security Groups, and 1 S3 Gateway Endpoint. 4 Apply Core Infrastructure Switch to profile nutrition-apply and apply the plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-apply" terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev apply tfplan Architecture Note: The dev root module simultaneously provisions network, RDS, and Cognito in an idle state (app_running = false). Do not use -target flags as this can disrupt Terraform state dependency graphs. 5 Verify Resources in AWS Console Sign in to AWS Console and navigate to VPC → Your VPCs:
Confirm VPC nutrition-dev-vpc exists with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Confirm 2 Public Subnets and 2 Private DB Subnets across 2 Availability Zones. Confirm Internet Gateway attached to the VPC. Verify DB route table contains no routes toward 0.0.0.0/0. Verify the 3 Security Groups: nutrition-dev-alb, nutrition-dev-ecs, and nutrition-dev-rds. Confirm S3 Gateway Endpoint status is Available. D. Evidence Screenshots Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/vpc-resource-map.png Figure 5.3.1.1. VPC Resource Map Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.1.1. VPC Resource Map: AWS VPC console displaying VPC CIDR, subnets, and routing table associations. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/vpc-security-groups.png Figure 5.3.1.2. System Security Groups Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.1.2. System Security Groups: Ingress and egress rules for ALB, ECS, and RDS security groups. E. Results Verification ✓ VPC and subnets deployed across 2 Availability Zones. ✓ ALB and ECS enforce proper security group isolation and designated ports. ✓ RDS allows PostgreSQL connections exclusively from ECS tasks. ✓ Route tables strictly separate public and database tiers. ✓ S3 Gateway Endpoint status is Available. F. Security Notice Never include real AWS Account IDs, sensitive IPs, or internal secrets in public documentation or screenshots. 5.3.2. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Database A. Learning Objectives Provision PostgreSQL 17 on Amazon RDS, enforce zero public exposure, and automate database schema evolution using Flyway migrations. B. Database Specifications Amazon RDS PostgreSQL configuration parameters in the dev environment: Property Configured Value Service Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (Engine version 17.x) Instance Class db.t4g.micro (AWS Graviton2 ARM architecture, cost-optimized) Storage 20 GB gp3 (Autoscaling up to 100 GB) Availability Single-AZ (default for demo savings, supports Multi-AZ via rds_multi_az) Subnet Group Private database subnets (nutrition-dev-db) Public Access Disabled (publicly_accessible = false) Encryption Enabled with AWS KMS (storage_encrypted = true) Credential Management AWS Secrets Manager managed password (manage_master_user_password = true) Schema Migration Flyway migrations V1–V11 executed by Spring Boot Key Security Properties: RDS cannot be reached from the Internet, preventing public exposure and credential attacks. Security Group accepts inbound traffic on PostgreSQL port (5432) exclusively from nutrition-dev-ecs tasks. Master password is generated and rotated automatically by Secrets Manager, never stored as plaintext in code or tfstate. Flyway guarantees deterministic, versioned schema state. C. Step-by-Step Implementation 1 Review Terraform RDS Module Inspect infra/modules/rds/main.tf for essential security directives:
HCLCopy manage_master_user_password = true db_subnet_group_name = aws_db_subnet_group.main.name vpc_security_group_ids = [var.security_group_id] publicly_accessible = false multi_az = var.multi_az
manage_master_user_password = true delegates database credentials to Secrets Manager directly.
2 Verify DB Subnet Group and Security Group Ensure aws_db_subnet_group.main binds the 2 private DB subnets and attaches the RDS security group from the network module.
3 Deploy via Terraform RDS PostgreSQL was provisioned during the root apply step in Lab 5.3.1. Initialization typically takes 5–8 minutes.
4 Inspect RDS in AWS Console Navigate to Amazon RDS → Databases and select nutrition-dev-postgres:
Status: Available (when app is running) or Stopped (during idle demo periods). Engine version: PostgreSQL 17.x. Instance: db.t4g.micro | Storage: 20 GB gp3. Multi-AZ: No (Single-AZ). Public access: No. Security Group: nutrition-dev-rds. 5 Verify Secrets Manager Metadata Navigate to AWS Secrets Manager and verify the managed secret matching rds!db-.... Do not open or reveal the plaintext secret value.
6 Review Flyway Migration Structure Inspect backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/ for SQL migration files V1 through V11:
V1__catalog.sql: Categories, products, and allergens tables. V3__commerce.sql: Orders, order items, and shopping cart tables. V4__chat_usage.sql: Chatbot usage limits table. V5__product_images.sql: Product image S3 keys. V6–V8: Expanded allergens and Vietnamese unaccent search. V9__payments.sql: Payment transaction entities. V10__payment_events.sql: Idempotent payment webhook events. V11__nutrition_profiles.sql: Personalized user nutrition profiles. When backend tasks launch on ECS, Flyway reads flyway_schema_history and automatically applies pending migrations.
D. Evidence Screenshots Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/rds-configuration.png Figure 5.3.2.1. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Configuration Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.2.1. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Configuration: RDS dashboard displaying PostgreSQL 17, db.t4g.micro instance class, and encryption status. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/rds-connectivity.png Figure 5.3.2.2. RDS Connectivity & Security Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.2.2. RDS Connectivity & Security: Private subnet group binding, security group isolation, and disabled public accessibility. E. Results Verification ✓ RDS PostgreSQL 17 provisioned with instance class db.t4g.micro. ✓ Public access is disabled. ✓ Storage encryption with AWS KMS is active. ✓ Port 5432 ingress permitted strictly from ECS security group. ✓ Flyway migrations ready to execute upon application startup. F. Common Issues & Operational Runbook Terraform cannot resume stopped RDS instances: The AWS RDS API prevents Terraform from transitioning an instance from stopped to available during standard apply calls. Operational Solution (per docs/runbook.md): Use the automated lifecycle script: PowerShellCopy powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .scriptsdemo-infra.ps1 up The script invokes AWS CLI to start the RDS instance, awaits Available state, and then invokes Terraform apply. 5.3.3. Amazon Cognito Authentication A. Learning Objectives Provision a centralized user authentication system, issue JWT tokens, and enforce Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). B. Cognito Architecture According to system security architecture: User Pool (nutrition-dev-users): Email-based user identification, automated verification email dispatch, and strong password enforcement (8+ chars, uppercase, lowercase, numbers, symbols). App Client (nutrition-dev-spa): Designed for Single Page Applications (React SPA) with generate_secret = false because browser clients cannot securely hold secret keys. Authentication Flows: Utilizes Secure Remote Password protocol (ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH) and refresh tokens (ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH). Does not use Cognito Hosted UI, opting for embedded React authentication screens. User Groups: Two pre-configured groups: USER (customers) and ADMIN (store administrators). Backend JWT Verification: Spring Boot Resource Server verifies JWT cryptographic signatures against Cognito JWKS, extracting user identity from claim sub and authorities from claim cognito:groups. C. Step-by-Step Implementation 1 Review Cognito Terraform Module Inspect infra/modules/cognito/main.tf for User Pool, App Client, and recovery settings:
HCLCopy resource "aws_cognito_user_pool_client" "spa" { name = "${var.name_prefix}-spa" user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.users.id generate_secret = false explicit_auth_flows = [ “ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH”, “ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH”, “ALLOW_ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH”, ] }
2 Review USER and ADMIN User Groups Verify user group definitions in infra/modules/cognito/main.tf:
HCLCopy resource "aws_cognito_user_group" "admin" { name = "ADMIN" user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.users.id } resource “aws_cognito_user_group” “user” { name = “USER” user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.users.id }
Registered users belong to USER. Only users assigned to ADMIN are granted access to administrative order and catalog endpoints.
3 Deploy Cognito Module Cognito is managed as code and provisioned during the root apply step. Do not manually create user pools in the AWS Console to avoid state drift.
4 Inspect Cognito in AWS Console Navigate to Amazon Cognito → User pools and select nutrition-dev-users:
Verify User Pool ID prefix: ap-southeast-1_.... Under App integration → App clients: Verify client nutrition-dev-spa with No client secret. Under Groups: Verify ADMIN and USER groups exist. 5 Verify API Authorization Enforcement (per docs/demo.md) Verify backend Spring Boot RBAC enforcement against incoming API calls:
Unauthenticated Requests: Calling protected endpoints without an Authorization: Bearer <token> header responds with HTTP 401 Unauthorized. Standard User accessing Admin API: A user in group USER attempting to access /api/admin/** triggers a claim inspection on cognito:groups and responds with HTTP 403 Forbidden. Admin User: Validated successfully and granted administrative permissions. D. Evidence Screenshots Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.3-core-infra/cognito-user-groups.png Figure 5.3.3.1. USER and ADMIN Groups in Amazon Cognito Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.3.3.1. USER and ADMIN Groups in Amazon Cognito: AWS Cognito console displaying configured user pool groups. E. Results Verification ✓ Cognito User Pool and SPA Client provisioned. ✓ Client Secret disabled for browser client security. ✓ USER and ADMIN groups created. ✓ JWT tokens validated by backend with HTTP 401 / 403 access control. ← 5.2 Prerequisites 5.4 App Deployment → 5.4 – Application Deployment 1. Learning Objectives Package Spring Boot 4 into an ARM64-optimized Docker container image. Authenticate with Amazon ECR and push the backend container image. Deploy the ECS Fargate service with 1 active task wired to the ALB. Compile the React 19 frontend and synchronize assets to Amazon S3 / CloudFront. 2. Prerequisites Completed Lab 5.3 (infrastructure outputs available).
3. Step-by-Step Practical Steps 1 Package Spring Boot Backend & Push to ECR Compile the JAR file and build the linux/arm64 Docker image:
TerminalCopy # 1. Build JAR package cd backend ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests 2. Extract ECR URL cd ../infra/envs/dev ECR_URL=$(terraform output -raw ecr_repository_url) cd ../../../backend
3. Authenticate Docker with ECR aws ecr get-login-password –region ap-southeast-1 | docker login –username AWS –password-stdin $ECR_URL
4. Build ARM64 Docker container image docker build –platform linux/arm64 -t $ECR_URL:latest .
5. Push image to Amazon ECR docker push $ECR_URL:latest
2 Start ECS Service & Launch Active Task Apply Terraform with app_running=true to spin up the ALB and ECS Fargate task:
TerminalCopy cd ../infra/envs/dev terraform apply -var="app_running=true" -var="api_desired_count=1" -auto-approve 3 Build & Deploy React Frontend to S3 Build the React SPA bundle and invalidate the CloudFront edge cache:
TerminalCopy cd ../../../frontend npm install npm run build cd ../infra/envs/dev FRONTEND_BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw frontend_bucket_name) DIST_ID=$(terraform output -raw cloudfront_distribution_id) cd ../../../frontend
aws s3 sync dist/ s3://$FRONTEND_BUCKET/ –delete aws cloudfront create-invalidation –distribution-id $DIST_ID –paths “/*"
Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.4-deployment/ecr-image-push.png Backend Image Pushed to Amazon ECR Evidence screenshot will be updated. Backend Image Pushed to Amazon ECR: ECR Console displaying the pushed container image with latest tag and scan results. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.4-deployment/ecs-task-running.png ECS Fargate Task in RUNNING State Evidence screenshot will be updated. ECS Fargate Task in RUNNING State: ECS Console displaying 1 healthy running container task in nutrition-dev-cluster. title: Project Proposal
content:
Project Proposal Architecture design, scope, problem statement, timeline, and cost estimate for the workshop project.
Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS Sourced nutrition lookup and shopping on AWS infrastructure
1. Proposal Summary The personalized nutrition e-commerce platform on AWS supports food lookup, purchasing, and meal recommendations from sourced data. React invokes Spring Boot via CloudFront and ALB; PostgreSQL stores data, while Bedrock only interprets requests. Products with missing data are excluded during nutrition or allergen filtering. Response metrics are retrieved by code directly from the DB, combined with demo-session-based operation to control costs.
2. Problem Statement What is the problem? Buyers struggle to compare food products when nutrition and allergen data are inconsistent. AI responses may contain unfounded figures if the model generates content autonomously.
Solution Buyers struggle to cross-reference nutrition and allergen data across products. Text-generating chatbots can produce unfounded figures. The MVP includes a catalog of 152 USDA products, accounts, filtering by nutrition, 9 allergens, and 6 diet labels; meal analysis; read-only AI lookup; shopping cart, ordering, product management, images, orders, analytics, and payment logs. COD and VNPAY sandbox are within scope.
D32 adds profiles and single-meal recommendations consisting of a protein dish, vegetables/fruit, and carbohydrates. Targets are calculated using Mifflin-St Jeor × activity level. Applicable only for ages 18–65, BMI 17–35, excluding pregnancy, lactation, and conditions requiring medical supervision. There are no real payments, automated refunds, or medical advice. Identity is extracted from JWT; inventory deduction uses conditional UPDATE within transactions.
Benefits and Return on Investment Buyers look up information from the DB, filter according to needs, and view data limitations. Store owners manage catalog, images, orders, and payment logs within the same application. Cost Explorer recorded 6.44 USD for Nov 01–21, 2026, fully covered by credits. There are no revenue or labor-saving figures yet to calculate financial ROI.
3. Solution Architecture AWS architecture reference Click on the image to expand / interactive zoom
AWS architecture diagram drawn on draw.io using AWS Architecture Icons, updated with Multi-AZ and AWS STS on Nov 25, 2026 From Nov 22, 2026 (D33), the dev environment runs 2 ECS tasks, one task per Availability Zone, and RDS in Multi-AZ mode with a standby replica in the second AZ. Reboot with failover drill on Nov 22 switched the primary AZ from ap-southeast-1a to ap-southeast-1b in about 20–45 seconds; API experienced roughly half a minute of disruption then automatically recovered, with zero data loss.
AWS services used CloudFront + S3 — React SPA and images via OAC; Function for path rewrites; two private buckets.
ALB + ECS Fargate + ECR — ALB accepts CloudFront + secret header; Spring Boot 4 / Java 21, ARM64, 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, 2 tasks across 2 AZs.
RDS PostgreSQL + Secrets Manager — db.t4g.micro, 20 GB gp3, Multi-AZ (standby in the second AZ), private subnet, encrypted; Flyway V1–V11.
Cognito — JWT sub and cognito:groups; USER / ADMIN.
Bedrock + Guardrails — Nova 2 Lite in Tokyo; read-only tools, metrics retrieved by code from the DB.
CloudWatch + SNS + Budgets — 14-day logs, 7 alarms, email alerts; 100 USD budget.
CloudTrail + S3 audit + WAF — Audit and ALB logs retained for 30 days; WAF only enabled during demo; AWS-managed KMS.
Terraform + IAM + STS + GitHub Actions — S3 state use_lockfile; SSO, boundary; CI/CD via OIDC, AWS STS grants temporary credentials (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity), no static access keys stored.
Application deployed in ap-southeast-1, prefix nutrition-dev, single dev environment. D15 places ECS in public subnets with public IP to avoid NAT costs, while RDS remains private. D17 chooses a single environment to fit the capstone project. D18 shifts Bedrock and Guardrail invocations to ap-northeast-1 because Singapore quota for the account is 0; profile jp.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0. D24/D31 restricts model to searchProducts with search, facts, compare, plan intents; metrics are assembled by the backend. CloudFront → ALB currently uses HTTP due to lack of a custom domain.
Component design Frontend React + TypeScript displays catalog, shopping cart, profiles, recommendations, and admin dashboard.
Backend Spring Boot 4 / Java 21: catalog manages lookups; commerce handles cart/orders; payments verifies IPN; ai extracts intent; admin provides management APIs; profile calculates targets and recommendations.
Database PostgreSQL uses parameterized SQL and Flyway V1–V11.
AI uses Nova 2 Lite with Guardrails; code validates filters and aggregates metrics from DB.
CI/CD GitHub Actions runs tests, builds ARM64, obtains temporary credentials from AWS STS via OIDC, pushes to ECR, and deploys.
4. Technical Implementation Terraform provisions infrastructure; Maven wrapper and Flyway manage backend/schema; React + TypeScript builds frontend. OIDC pipeline builds, tests, and deploys along the master branch. Phases are grouped according to milestones recorded in the repository.
Phase 2026 Timeline Actual Scope 1 Oct 29–Nov 01 Repository, frontend skeleton, catalog backend, Cognito 2 Nov 03–10 UI design, USDA data 3 Nov 11–12 Terraform network/RDS/ECR/Cognito/ALB/ECS/CloudFront; OIDC; first AWS run 4 Nov 13–18 AI, Guardrails, alarms; search, rate limiting, meal analysis, VNPAY sandbox, UI 5 Nov 20–22 Tokyo, E2E, audit/optional WAF; AI full intent, D32, audit apply and cost measurement 5. Implementation Plan and Milestones Date Actual Milestone 29/10/2026 Repository initialization 01/11/2026 Frontend skeleton, catalog backend, Cognito 03–06/11/2026 UI redesign 10/11/2026 USDA data 11/11/2026 Terraform networking, RDS, ECR, Cognito, ALB, ECS, and CloudFront 12/11/2026 OIDC, product images, and first AWS run 13/11/2026 AI, Guardrails, evaluation, and alarms 14–15/11/2026 Search, password reset, statistics, rate limiting, Spring Boot 4 16/11/2026 Catalog expansion, diet labels, meal analysis, VNPAY sandbox 17–18/11/2026 UI finalization 20/11/2026 Tokyo, E2E, audit, optional WAF, payment logs 21/11/2026 AI full intent, profiles, and D32 recommendations 22/11/2026 Audit apply and cost measurement 6. Budget Estimate Infrastructure cost Estimated USD/month, cross-referenced with AWS Pricing Calculator on Nov 25, 2026 for Multi-AZ configuration and 2 tasks (D33), exclusive of tax, variance may be ±10%. Production is a future proposal not yet deployed. Bedrock actually invoked in Tokyo.
Service / Configuration Demo (~4h/day) 24/7 (Pricing Calculator) Proposed Production RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.micro, Multi-AZ, 20 GB gp3 ~11.6 42.75 ~70 (Multi-AZ, db.t4g.small) ECS Fargate ARM64, 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, 2 tasks ~5.9 35.98 ~36–72 (2–4 tasks, auto scaling) Application Load Balancer ~3.1 18.63 ~22 Public IPv4, 4 addresses ~2.4 14.60 ~15 Secrets Manager, 2 secrets 0.85 0.85 0.85 Bedrock (Nova Lite as pricing reference, Tokyo) <0.7 0.70 Based on usage CloudFront 1.02 · CloudWatch 1.70 · ECR 0.10 · S3 0.07 · Cognito 0 · CloudTrail 0 ~2.9 2.89 ~5 Total (without WAF) ~27 116.40 ~150–190 WAF (optional, Optional group) 0 9.60 ~10 Total with WAF — 126.00 ~160–200 Cost Explorer recorded 6.44 USD for Nov 01–21, 2026, fully covered by credits. RDS 2.77; ALB 1.29; ECS 1.21; IPv4 0.74; Bedrock 0.21; Secrets Manager 0.20 USD. The listed items represent the major charges, not an itemized sum of the entire invoice. Since the app is only turned on during demo sessions, these actual numbers must not be used to extrapolate 24/7 operation. These actual figures were recorded before enabling Multi-AZ.
AWS Pricing Calculator estimate dated Nov 25, 2026. The 24/7 column uses the exact figures from Calculator (Singapore, except Bedrock in Tokyo). The Demo column converts from that for approximately 120 operating hours per month: hourly charges (RDS instance, Fargate, ALB, IPv4) multiplied by 120/730, while RDS storage (5.52 USD) and usage-based items remain unchanged. Load assumptions: 50 users/month, 5 GB CloudFront, approximately 3,600 AI queries/month (1 query/minute for 2 hours/day, 1,500 input tokens, 300 output tokens). Since the Calculator did not yet list Amazon Nova 2 Lite, Amazon Nova Lite was used as the pricing reference. The estimate excludes RDS Proxy and Database Insights Advanced as they are not used by the project.
7. Risk Assessment Risk matrix Risk Impact Probability Level Unexpected cost Medium Medium Medium Personal data exposure High Low Medium AI incorrect/medical response High Medium High Bedrock quota Medium High (already occurred in Singapore) Medium HTTP from CloudFront to ALB Medium Low Low Single Availability Zone failure High Low Medium (reduced via Multi-AZ) Scoring methodology: Impact and Probability are evaluated across three levels: Low / Medium / High; Level is a combination of the two factors, after factoring in mitigation measures below. AI risk is classified as High because incorrect nutrition figures or medical advice can affect user health, thus prioritized for multi-layered controls.
Mitigation measures Cost: 100 USD Budgets, alarms, and up/down scripts. RDS may automatically turn back on after 7 days stopped.
Personal data: JWT and authorization; avoid logging PII, physical biometric data is not sent to the model; users can delete their own profiles.
AI: Guardrails, read-only tools, metrics from DB; evaluation of 45 queries on Nov 21, 2026 achieved 17/17 safety, 27/28 lookup, 85% threshold. Query L01 still fluctuates.
Quota: Tokyo replaces Singapore per D18; monitor ApplyGuardrail permissions.
Origin: CloudFront prefix list and secret header reduce direct access; HTTP to ALB remains a constraint. HTTPS origin will require a custom domain and certificate in the future.
Contingency plan When Bedrock is unreachable, maintain catalog and shopping flows, returning controlled AI errors. If costs rise, scale down following the runbook. When DB restoration is needed, follow the snapshot procedure in docs/runbook.md; drill record still awaits repository owner execution.
8. Expected Outcomes Technical improvements: React Web and API on CloudFront.
Source code, tests, and OIDC workflow on GitHub.
Terraform and demo-session operational guidelines.
Workshop package with 7 major sections, sub-steps, and bilingual report.

content:
Technical Workshop Guide Deploying Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS Hands-on Deployment Guide: Spring Boot 4, React 19, ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL, Bedrock AI & Terraform
A comprehensive step-by-step practical lab guide enabling engineers and students to deploy an end-to-end cloud-native nutrition e-commerce platform on Amazon Web Services. The entire infrastructure is automated via Terraform, running containerized Spring Boot 4 backend on serverless ECS Fargate, managed PostgreSQL on RDS, and generative AI intent parsing with Amazon Bedrock Nova 2 Lite. 5.1 Overview 5.2 Prerequisites 5.3 Core Infra 5.4 App Deployment 5.5 Bedrock AI 5.6 Monitoring & Cost 5.7 Clean-up 5.1. Workshop Overview Building a Personalized Nutrition E-Commerce Platform on AWS This workshop guides you through deploying a cloud-native nutrition e-commerce platform on AWS using React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL, integrated with Amazon Bedrock for natural language food search. Learners will practice provisioning infrastructure, deploying application workloads, integrating AI capabilities, monitoring systems, and managing AWS cloud costs. Workshop Objectives Understand cloud web application architecture on AWS. Deploy frontend, backend, and managed database tiers. Integrate Amazon Bedrock for AI-assisted nutritional queries. Establish monitoring, security controls, and cost optimization. Overall Architecture Overall Architecture Diagram of Nutrition E-Commerce on AWS. The React application is distributed globally via CloudFront and S3. API requests are routed through an Application Load Balancer to Spring Boot on ECS Fargate. PostgreSQL is hosted on Amazon RDS, Cognito manages user authentication, and Amazon Bedrock powers nutritional intent extraction. Core application infrastructure is hosted in Singapore, with Bedrock and Guardrails operating in Tokyo. Workshop Roadmap 5.2. Prerequisites: Prepare AWS Account and developer toolchain. 5.3. Core Infrastructure: Provision cloud resources using Terraform. 5.4. Application Deployment: Deploy React and Spring Boot to AWS. 5.5. Amazon Bedrock: Integrate AI conversational nutrition search. 5.6. Monitoring & Cost: Configure observability, security, and budgets. 5.7. Resource Cleanup: Stop or tear down resources after the workshop. Expected Outcome Upon completing this workshop, learners will be capable of deploying, operating, and testing an AI-enabled nutrition e-commerce system on AWS while understanding how to monitor and control cloud expenditures. 5.2 Prerequisites → 5.2 – Prerequisites & Environment Setup Before deploying the Nutrition E-Commerce platform on AWS, learners must prepare an AWS account, developer toolchains, IAM access permissions, and a remote storage backend for Terraform State. This hands-on lab guides you through environment verification, configuring AWS IAM Identity Center, and bootstrapping the Terraform Backend on Amazon S3. 5.2.1. Tooling Preparation The table below lists the required developer toolchains and runtimes: Tool Requirement AWS Account Permissions to configure required AWS services (VPC, ECS, RDS, IAM, CloudFront, Bedrock) AWS CLI Version 2 (AWS CLI v2.x) Terraform Version ≥ 1.10 (tested with Terraform v1.10.5) Java JDK 21 (Eclipse Temurin or OpenJDK 21) Node.js & npm Compatible with repository (Node.js ≥ 20.x or 22.x LTS, npm ≥ 10.x) Docker Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with multi-platform container build support (linux/arm64) Git Source code version control (Git ≥ 2.40.x) PowerShell PowerShell 7 or Windows PowerShell for running verification commands and lifecycle scripts on Windows 5.2.2. Configure AWS Access & IAM Infrastructure provisioning adheres strictly to the Least Privilege principle with the following IAM components: AWS IAM Identity Center: Centrally manages user authentication and role assignments to AWS accounts via Single Sign-On (SSO). Permission set nutrition-plan: Attached with AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess, used for daily inspection, syntax validation, and planning (terraform plan). Permission set nutrition-apply: Combines ReadOnlyAccess with an inline policy from nutrition-apply-policy.json to apply approved infrastructure changes. Policy nutrition-boundary: Enforces a maximum permission boundary (nutrition-boundary-policy.json) on all IAM roles generated by Terraform (ECS task roles, execution roles, GitHub Actions OIDC roles). Configuration and Verification Steps (per docs/aws-setup/README.md): Log in to the AWS Management Console with administrative privileges (Root or Admin). Open IAM Policies and create policy nutrition-boundary pasting docs/aws-setup/nutrition-boundary-policy.json. Verify that Access Analyzer reports zero validation errors. Open IAM Identity Center → Permission sets: Create permission set nutrition-plan attaching AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess. Create permission set nutrition-apply attaching ReadOnlyAccess and pasting docs/aws-setup/nutrition-apply-policy.json into the Inline Policy. Set session duration to 4 hours. Assign both permission sets to your designated IAM Identity Center user on the target AWS account. Verify regional isolation constraints: Core services are restricted to ap-southeast-1 (Singapore); CloudFront is global and S3 is restricted to nutrition-* buckets; an exception in ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) is granted exclusively for Amazon Bedrock and Guardrails. Security Notice: Never attach unrestricted AdministratorAccess. The project enforces an IAM Permission Boundary to cap maximum permissions and prevent unintended privilege escalation. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/iam-permission-sets.png Figure 5.2.1. Permission Sets in AWS IAM Identity Center Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.1. Permission Sets in AWS IAM Identity Center: Configuration of nutrition-plan and nutrition-apply permission sets in Identity Center. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/iam-permission-boundary.png Figure 5.2.2. IAM Permission Boundary for Project Roles Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.2. IAM Permission Boundary for Project Roles: The nutrition-boundary policy bounding maximum permissions for application roles. 5.2.3. AWS CLI SSO Login Authenticate your AWS CLI session using the pre-configured SSO session name nutrition: PowerShellCopy aws sso login --sso-session nutrition After completing browser authentication, verify your active identity with profile nutrition-plan: PowerShellCopy aws sts get-caller-identity --profile nutrition-plan Expected Output: The command responds with a valid JSON document containing UserId, Account, and Arn corresponding to your permission set. (For security reasons, actual Account IDs and sensitive data are sanitized and omitted from public documentation). Troubleshooting InvalidGrantException: This error indicates an expired SSO token session. Re-authenticate by executing aws sso login --sso-session nutrition to obtain a fresh token. 5.2.4. Bootstrap Terraform Backend on S3 Terraform State preserves the current state of AWS infrastructure managed by Terraform. The project uses Amazon S3 as a Remote Backend with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 AES256), Versioning enabled, and native state locking via use_lockfile = true (introduced in Terraform 1.10+, eliminating the need for a DynamoDB table). Follow the step-by-step instructions from infra/README.md: 1 Initialize Terraform Bootstrap Navigate to the bootstrap directory and download required providers:
PowerShellCopy terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap init 2 Review Terraform Plan Set the owner variable and save the binary execution plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:TF_VAR_owner = "your-name" terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap plan -out=tfplan Review the planned resources carefully to confirm that only intended S3 state bucket components will be created before proceeding to apply. 3 Deploy Bootstrap Switch to the nutrition-apply profile and apply the saved plan:
PowerShellCopy $env:AWS_PROFILE = "nutrition-apply" terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap apply tfplan 4 Retrieve State Bucket Name Query the created S3 state bucket name from Terraform output:
PowerShellCopy terraform -chdir=infra/bootstrap output state_bucket The output displays a unique bucket name formatted as: nutrition-dev-tfstate-<account-id>.
5 Configure Dev Environment Backend Copy the backend template file from the dev environment folder and populate the bucket name:
PowerShellCopy cp infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl.example infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl Configured content inside infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl:
HCLCopy bucket = "nutrition-dev-tfstate-<account-id>" Key S3 Remote Backend Features: Terraform State is stored securely with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 AES256) and TLS enforcement. use_lockfile = true provides robust native state locking directly on S3 objects, preventing concurrent write collisions. The bucket is protected by prevent_destroy = true in the bootstrap definition to guard against accidental removal. AWS Budgets Advisory: Prior to deploying chargeable resources, learners should configure budget alert thresholds in AWS Budgets. The team project adheres to a 100 USD benchmark limit. Detailed step-by-step setup, email alerts, and screenshot evidence are covered in Module 5.6 – Monitoring, Security & Cost. Note that the bootstrap module does not automatically create AWS Budgets. Evidence Screenshot assets/images/workshop/5.2-prerequisites/terraform-state-s3.png Figure 5.2.3. Amazon S3 Bucket for Terraform State Evidence screenshot will be updated. Figure 5.2.3. Amazon S3 Bucket for Terraform State: S3 bucket nutrition-dev-tfstate with SSE-S3 encryption and use_lockfile native locking. 5.2.5. Results Verification Verify the following checklist before proceeding to infrastructure provisioning: ✓ AWS CLI successfully authenticated via SSO with return exit code 0. ✓ Profiles nutrition-plan and nutrition-apply configured correctly in AWS config. ✓ The nutrition-boundary policy exists and passes IAM Policy Validation. ✓ Terraform Bootstrap initialized and applied without permission errors. ✓ S3 Remote State bucket created in Singapore (ap-southeast-1) with encryption and public access blocks. ✓ Configuration in infra/envs/dev/backend.hcl correctly matches the actual state bucket name. ✓ No sensitive access keys or real account IDs are committed to version control. 5.2.6. These components provide the foundational infrastructure required for deploying the Spring Boot backend in subsequent steps. 5.3.1. VPC Networking A. Learning Objectives Deploy segmented network infrastructure for backend services and databases, ensuring Application Load Balancer (ALB), ECS Fargate, and RDS operate within appropriate network boundaries while eliminating NAT Gateway costs. B. Network Architecture According to project architectural decisions (D15 & D19), the network comprises: One VPC in Singapore (ap-southeast-1), with default CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 spanned across 2 Availability Zones. Two Public Subnets (10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24) hosting the ALB and ECS Fargate container tasks. Two Private Database Subnets (10.0.100.0/24 and 10.0.101.0/24) dedicated to Amazon RDS with zero direct Internet routing. An Internet Gateway (IGW) attached to the VPC. Route Tables: Public route table directs 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW; database route table restricts traffic strictly to internal VPC CIDRs. S3 Gateway Endpoint: Enables ECS tasks to transfer product media with Amazon S3 over AWS internal network at zero hourly cost, bypassing the Internet Gateway. CloudFront Origin-Facing Managed Prefix List: Restricts ALB ingress exclusively to CloudFront CDN origin-facing IP ranges. Three-Tier Security Group Isolation: ALB Security Group (nutrition-dev-alb): Ingress accepts HTTP (port 80) only from CloudFront Managed Prefix List; Egress forwards traffic only to ECS tasks on port 8080. ECS Security Group (nutrition-dev-ecs): Ingress accepts application traffic (port 8080) only from ALB SG; Egress allows port 5432 to RDS SG and HTTPS (port 443) outbound to AWS APIs (ECR, Bedrock, Cognito JWKS, CloudWatch). RDS Security Group (nutrition-dev-rds): Ingress permits PostgreSQL traffic (port 5432) strictly from ECS SG; direct Internet ingress is completely forbidden. C. HCLCopy data "aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list" "cloudfront" { name = "com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing" } This ensures ALB only accepts incoming requests originating from CloudFront edge distributions.
2 Review Terraform Variables Verify parameters passed into module network from infra/envs/dev/main.tf:
name_prefix = "nutrition-dev": Unified naming prefix. enable_nat = false: Disables NAT Gateway by default to prevent hourly billing (~$32/month). ECS tasks assign public IPs in public subnets to communicate outbound with AWS APIs. 3 Generate and Review Terraform Plan Authenticate with profile nutrition-plan and generate an execution plan:

Do not use -target flags as this can disrupt Terraform state dependency graphs. 5 Verify Resources in AWS Console Sign in to AWS Console and navigate to VPC → Your VPCs:
Confirm VPC nutrition-dev-vpc exists with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Confirm 2 Public Subnets and 2 Private DB Subnets across 2 Availability Zones. Confirm Internet Gateway attached to the VPC. Verify DB route table contains no routes toward 0.0.0.0/0. Verify the 3 Security Groups: nutrition-dev-alb, nutrition-dev-ecs, and nutrition-dev-rds. Confirm S3 Gateway Endpoint status is Available. Security Group accepts inbound traffic on PostgreSQL port (5432) exclusively from nutrition-dev-ecs tasks. Master password is generated and rotated automatically by Secrets Manager, never stored as plaintext in code or tfstate. Flyway guarantees deterministic, versioned schema state. C. title: EC2 Identity Containment
content:
← Back to Articles AWS STUDY GROUP / CLOUD SECURITY EC2 ISOLATION DOES NOT MEAN THE ATTACKER IS ISOLATED Beyond Network Isolation: Rethinking Identity Containment on AWS View post on AWS Study Group VN community 15/11/2026 Figure 1: Automated Incident Response architecture on AWS – Combining Network Containment, Credential Issuance Containment, and Identity Containment. What happens if an EC2 instance is completely isolated from the network, yet an attacker can still access your AWS resources? An in-depth architectural analysis of Network Containment versus Identity Containment: why Security Groups cannot terminate active IAM sessions, the limitations of IMDSv2 against remote code execution, and designing an automated incident response workflow combining GuardDuty, EventBridge, Lambda runbooks, and aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC condition keys.
1. When What Is Stolen Is Not Just Data, But Identity Consider an enterprise deploying its backend workload on Amazon EC2, using Amazon S3 for durable object storage and Amazon DynamoDB for transactional state.
Rather than embedding long-lived Access Keys into source code, EC2 is attached to an IAM Role via an Instance Profile, consuming Temporary Security Credentials issued dynamically by the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS).
While this aligns with AWS security best practices, examine this realistic incident timeline:
Time Event / Action Technical Implication & State 09:00 EC2 Host Compromise Attacker exploits an application vulnerability to achieve arbitrary remote code execution (RCE) on the host. 09:05 Credentials Exfiltration Attacker queries IMDS and extracts temporary security tokens (AccessKey, SecretKey, SessionToken). 09:10 Security Team Detects Anomaly Security operations center (SOC) detects suspicious host behavior or unexpected API calls. 09:15 Quarantine Security Group Applied EC2 is isolated at the network layer by stripping standard inbound and outbound traffic rules. 09:20 Attacker Accesses S3 from Outside From an external Internet environment, the attacker successfully dispatches requests to Amazon S3 using the stolen credentials. Why does this happen? Because Temporary Credentials are not inherently bound to the network origin of the EC2 instance that received them. As long as the credentials have not expired and access has not been denied by security policies, an attacker can exploit the workload identity directly against AWS APIs without needing any ongoing network connection to the original EC2 instance. 2. Network Containment ≠ Identity Containment A critical pitfall in cloud incident response is failing to distinguish between two distinct control planes: Network Containment (isolating resources at the network perimeter) and Identity Containment (governing and revoking the operational permissions of compromised identities).
Control Layer Mechanism Capability Core Limitation Network Containment
Network Layer Quarantine Security Group, NACLs, Private Subnets Blocks network ingress/egress to and from the EC2 instance Cannot invalidate active IAM credentials; does not drop tracked stateful connections immediately. Identity Containment
Identity Layer (IAM) Revoke Active Sessions, Policy Denials, Detach Instance Profile Revokes operational validity of temporary STS credentials Without detaching the Instance Profile, the instance can immediately request new credentials from IMDS. Security Groups filter network ingress and egress traffic, but possess zero awareness or authority over IAM sessions. Furthermore, modifying a Security Group does not automatically terminate existing tracked stateful TCP connections.
Private Subnets prevent direct inbound connections from the public Internet, but do not protect against an attacker utilizing exfiltrated credentials from an external machine.
Even IMDSv2, while highly effective against Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) exploits, offers no protection once an attacker has established arbitrary code execution on the instance.
Each security mechanism addresses a different failure domain. Stacking security tools without understanding their architectural boundaries does not produce a secure architecture.
3. If Credentials Are Stolen, Can We Render Them Useless Out of Context? AWS provides Global Condition Keys that enable organizations to restrict credential usage based on operational context, verifying that request attributes match the issuance environment:
aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC: Enforces that requests must originate from the exact VPC where the EC2 instance was granted credentials. aws:EC2InstanceSourcePrivateIPv4: Verifies the private IPv4 address assigned to the instance when the credentials were issued. aws:SourceVpc: Checks whether the request passed through a specific VPC Endpoint when accessing AWS service APIs. aws:VpcSourceIp: Validates the source IP address within the private VPC network space. In the illustrated architecture, EC2 resides within a Private Subnet and connects to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB via dedicated Gateway Endpoints.
By authoring IAM Policies that compare credential issuance context with runtime request context, we can deny unauthorized requests originating outside the legitimate network boundary, even when the security token is valid.
Example: IAM Policy Deny access outside source VPC (Context-Aware Enforcement) { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "EnforceVpcSourceContext", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": ["s3:*", "dynamodb:*"], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC": "vpc-0123456789abcdef0" } } } ] } However, architects must keep in mind that not all AWS APIs utilize VPC Endpoints. Overly restrictive policies can break legitimate operational workloads.
This mechanism also does not prevent malicious actions carried out directly on the compromised EC2 instance itself.
This is why a robust cloud security strategy demands layered Defense in Depth.
4. When Security Remediation Causes Operational Outages AWS IAM provides an Active Session Revocation mechanism using the managed AWSRevokeOlderSessions policy and the aws:TokenIssueTime condition to deny requests from credentials issued prior to a specific cutoff timestamp.
However, imagine a production fleet where 10 EC2 instances share a single IAM Role, but only one instance has been compromised.
Executing a blanket session revocation on that IAM Role immediately disrupts all 9 healthy instances, inducing a widespread cascading outage.
Furthermore, Revoke Active Sessions does not stop the compromised EC2 from immediately querying IMDS for fresh credentials. Therefore, security teams must detach or swap the Instance Profile with a restricted quarantine profile.
At this point, engineering teams confront the delicate trade-off between Security and Availability.
This demonstrates that IAM architecture is not just about granting Least Privilege, but equally about strictly limiting the Blast Radius when an incident occurs.
5. Architectural Approach on AWS Synthesizing the architecture diagram, we can construct an Automated Incident Response workflow as follows:
AWS Service Role in Incident Response AWS CloudTrail Captures and records AWS API activity. Data Events must be enabled on S3 and DynamoDB for granular data-tier visibility. Amazon GuardDuty Continuously monitors security data sources to detect anomalous credential usage (e.g. InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding). Amazon EventBridge Matches GuardDuty finding event patterns and triggers automated incident response handlers. AWS Lambda Executes an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to carry out multi-tiered containment actions. The containment workflow executes across three synchronized action tiers:
Network Containment: Attaches a Quarantine Security Group and inspects existing stateful connections. Credential Issuance Containment: Detaches or swaps the Instance Profile to prevent the instance from receiving fresh privileged credentials. Identity Containment: Revokes active IAM Role sessions and verifies policy propagation across AWS endpoints. In production environments, actions that carry high operational disruption risks should be governed by appropriate approval workflows. The ultimate goal is not simply deploying more tools, but ensuring that each defensive layer successfully contains damage when another layer fails.
Key Takeaway An AWS Incident Response workflow must govern both Network Containment and Identity Containment simultaneously. Isolating EC2 only solves part of the problem if the operational permissions of the compromised identity have not been revoked. Because in cloud environments, an attack may begin on a host but propagates through identity abuse. #AWS #AWSStudyGroup #CloudSecurity #CyberSecurity #IAM #AmazonEC2 #GuardDuty #IncidentResponse #DefenseInDepth #CloudArchitecture Official Documentation & References AWS Security Incident Response Guide – Containment and Remediation Strategies: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/containment.html AWS IAM Documentation – Revoking IAM Role Temporary Security Credentials: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_revoke-sessions.html Amazon GuardDuty Finding Types – InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_finding-types-ec2.html View post on AWS Study Group VN community ← Back to Articles Scroll to Top ↑

Events Participated / Event 3 - First Cloud AI Journey Meetup (October 24, 2026) ← Back to Events EVENT HARVEST REPORT Cloud Computing, Cloud Security & AI Agents Official • AWS FCAJ FIRST CLOUD AI JOURNEY MEETUP Exploring AWS Cloud, Cloud Security, and the Future of AI Agents
Event Name: First Cloud AI Journey Meetup – 24/10/2026 Date & Time: 08:00 AM – 12:00 PM, October 24, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Speakers: Kiệt Trần, Long Huỳnh, Thịnh Nguyễn, Xuân An, Khoa Kiều, Nghi Danh Role: Attendee Authentic attendee check-in photograph at First Cloud AI Journey Meetup (October 24, 2026) – 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower 01 I. Event Overview The First Cloud AI Journey Meetup focused on five core technical domains: Voice AI, AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), AI-assisted Penetration Testing, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Kiro Crew.
Featured Speakers: Kiệt Trần, Long Huỳnh, Thịnh Nguyễn, Xuân An, Khoa Kiều, Nghi Danh “The meetup gathered technology leaders, solutions engineers, and the AWS community in Vietnam, presenting technical lectures, live architecture demonstrations, and discussions on practical cloud and artificial intelligence applications in enterprise environments.” The technical scope spanned real-time low-latency voice AI systems, secure cross-account cloud resource sharing, Shift-Left automated penetration testing, and production runtime environments and memory management for AI Agents.
02 II. Event Objectives Core technical and architectural objectives established during the meetup:
Explore practical applications of AWS Cloud and Artificial Intelligence: Present cutting-edge cloud and AI services deployed directly into production systems. Understand cloud resource sharing and security management: Analyze multi-account governance structured via AWS RAM, AWS Organizations, and SCPs. Learn about Voice AI and AI Agent architectures: Examine real-time bidirectional conversational workflows and agentic execution engines. Explore automated security testing and AI-powered development: Review Shift-Left Security methodologies and AI agents accelerating software engineering lifecycles. Connect with the AWS engineering community: Provide an open technical exchange among architects, industry engineers, and builders. 03 III. Event Content & Technical Sessions 1. Hear, Think, Speak – Building a Vietnamese Voice-AI Contact Center on AWS Speaker: Kiệt Trần – Revve AI The session focused on three primary criteria in engineering production Voice AI systems: Response Accuracy, Low Latency, and Natural Conversational Experience.
The live demonstration showcased an AI-powered voice interview screening Cloud Engineer candidates in Vietnamese, engineered to reduce end-to-end response latency to approximately 1.8 seconds for smooth conversational turn-taking.
Voice AI Processing Workflow Voice Input → Speech Recognition → AI Processing → Speech Generation → Voice Response Component Technical Function Hear Receive and process incoming user speech streams in real time. Think Interpret requests, query contextual knowledge, and generate appropriate responses. Speak Synthesize generated text responses into natural spoken language for playback. 2. AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) Speaker: Long Huỳnh – Styl Solution The second session addressed secure cross-account resource sharing across multiple AWS accounts within an enterprise organization.
AWS Resource Access Manager allows supported resources (VPC Subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 Resolver Rules) to be shared without requiring duplicated infrastructure across sub-accounts, reducing overhead and streamlining centralized management.
Key Components Component Primary Function AWS RAM Enables secure cross-account resource sharing across organizational accounts. AWS Organizations Supports centralized hierarchy, multi-account governance, and consolidated billing. IAM Policies Defines fine-grained access permissions for users and compute resources. Service Control Policies (SCPs) Establishes organization-level permission guardrails and maximum permission boundaries. 3. AWS Pentest with AWS Continuum / Security Agent Speaker: Thịnh Nguyễn – Styl Solution The third session introduced automated infrastructure security assessment and penetration testing assisted by AI Security Agents, emphasizing early vulnerability identification during the software development lifecycle (SDLC).
Shift-Left Security The Shift-Left Security methodology was outlined through four progressive validation checkpoints:
Reviewing Terraform infrastructure-as-code (IaC) definitions. Integrating automated security checks into GitHub and GitLab pull requests. Pinpointing misconfigurations and security exposures prior to deployment. Deploying AI Security Agents to execute automated penetration tests in authorized SIT and UAT environments. Security Assessment Workflow Source Code → Security Review → Testing Environment → Security Validation → Production Deployment 4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Speaker: Xuân An – Leader AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE The session focused on two primary architectural components of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: AgentCore Runtime and AgentCore Memory.
Associated technical topics addressed execution environments, context management, scalability, and operating AI Agents within production workloads.
4.1. AgentCore Runtime AgentCore Runtime provides a managed execution environment for deploying and operating AI Agents. Key architectural factors include:
Agent execution and workload isolation. Elastic infrastructure scalability matching demand. Optimized compute resource utilization. Enterprise production deployment requirements. 4.2. AgentCore Memory AgentCore Memory manages conversational context and persistent interaction states across multi-turn AI Agent workflows.
Memory Type Description Short-term Memory Maintains recent conversational context and immediate interaction history. Long-term Memory Retains persistent knowledge and preferences for cross-session retrieval. 5. Kiro Crew – AI-Powered Development and Automation Speakers: Khoa Kiều – Tech Lead, ACB & Nghi Danh – AWS Community Builder The final session explored how autonomous AI Agent groups support continuous software development, automated code inspection, and system status monitoring.
5.1. Artifact Generation The live demonstration showed AI Agents collecting real-world job postings, parsing data streams, and generating interactive visual reports and analytical charts directly within the workspace.
5.2. Context Window Management The speakers analyzed context window optimization techniques for long-running workflows via two core mechanisms:
Auto Compact: Automatically condenses conversation context as token usage approaches context limits. Context Breakdown: Analyzes token distribution across components to isolate context expansion factors. 5.3. Memory Management & Security Guardrails The presentation emphasized selective memory retention and establishing strict security guardrails preventing AI Agents from:
Deleting cloud infrastructure without explicit authorization. Exposing sensitive secrets, access keys, or API credentials. Performing unauthorized system or configuration modifications. Executing destructive or high-risk operations without human oversight. 04 IV. Key Takeaways The five technical sessions consolidated practical knowledge across foundational areas of Cloud Computing, AI, and Cloud Security:
Technical Area Key Architectural Concepts Voice AI Real-time voice processing and latency optimization (< 2s). AWS RAM Secure cross-account resource sharing across organizational accounts. AWS Organizations Centralized multi-account governance and organizational guardrails. Cloud Security Shift-Left Security and automated penetration testing. AgentCore Runtime Production execution environments and workload isolation for AI Agents. AgentCore Memory Short-term and long-term memory governance for multi-turn agent interactions. Kiro Crew AI-powered continuous development, code reviews, and system inspection. Context Management Token consumption governance and context optimization (Auto Compact, Context Breakdown). Security Guardrails Enforcing security guardrails preventing unauthorized or destructive AI actions. Core architectural principles established: Cloud and AI architectures must balance performance, security, and operational efficiency. Centralized resource sharing simplifies multi-account infrastructure management. Security assessments should be integrated directly into the software development lifecycle. Production AI Agents depend on reliable runtime environments and structured memory management. AI automation must operate strictly within verified security guardrails. 05 V. Lessons Learned & Personal Contributions 1. Lessons Learned Understand the importance of latency optimization in Voice AI systems. Recognize the benefits of centralized resource sharing and cloud governance. Understand the importance of integrating security into the software development lifecycle. Recognize the role of Runtime and Memory in production AI Agents. Understand the importance of security guardrails in AI automation. 2. Practical Applications Voice processing pipeline optimization: Research and apply cascade architectures (STT → LLM → TTS) with real-time buffering and WebRTC protocols in interactive conversational applications. Implement secure resource sharing: Apply AWS RAM and SCP guardrails to design secure multi-account VPC sharing topologies in cloud architecture coursework. Embed security linting in CI/CD: Incorporate automated Terraform IaC security checks into personal GitHub Actions workflows to identify misconfigurations before deployment. Govern context and guardrails for AI Agents: Implement Auto Compact, token breakdown metrics, and security guardrails when building AI agents on Amazon Bedrock. 3. Personal Contributions Participated in the meetup as an Attendee from 08:00 AM to 12:00 PM on October 24, 2026, at Bitexco Financial Tower. Followed technical presentations and live demonstrations across all technical sessions. Consolidated technical knowledge into a personal event report. Identified opportunities to apply cloud security and AI automation concepts in future learning activities. Built a detailed event report and published, shared technical knowledge transparently via the personal website and GitHub repository. 06 VI. Conclusion The First Cloud AI Journey Meetup on October 24, 2026, delivered substantial practical value regarding the convergence of Cloud Computing, Cloud Security, and Artificial Intelligence.
The meetup substantially broadened my technical mindset: recognizing that real-world AI deployment extends beyond simple conversational prompts to require reliable runtimes, structured context governance, and rigorous security boundaries. Furthermore, Shift-Left security practices and automated penetration testing reinforced the discipline of embedding cloud security directly into code from the start.
These insights establish vital guidance for advancing my specialized studies in AI Agents and AWS cloud infrastructure security in future learning milestones.
